                Chapter 45: Dragonstone: Works of Fire


It was a few moons of reprieve before the big evacuation of the Red Keep for wildfire
removal.

As Robert predicted, Cersei kicked up a giant fuss; she was adamantly not going to camp out
on the tourney grounds for moons at a time! Surely, if it must be done, they could go to a
proper castle to stay! Stannis quietly suggested to Robert that it would not be fair to burden
some unfortunate Crownlands lord with the costs of housing and feeding the royal court for
moons on end. Better a castle built for the purpose of ruling on a kingdom’s scale.

Storm’s End, perhaps? It was nearly empty now, with only the barest garrison and staff to
keep it going. Only it was so far away. Which made Casterly Rock right out, not that any of
the Baratheon brothers particularly wanted to be jammed in close quarters with Tywin
Lannister. The Eyrie was also regretfully dropped as a consideration by Robert due to the
distances; it was even less suitable as a place to hold central government. Harrenhall would
hold them all more than adequately and was central, but Robert wasn’t ashamed to admit that
the entire place creeped him out tremendously. He was not afraid of anybody trying to kill
him with normal weapons. Curses and hauntings, strange, unexplainable goings on in the
darkness of the night? What did he know about combating such things? Nope, nope, he
wasn’t staying in a place that had curses and other such things going on. Better safe than
sorry, that’s what.

The court would go to Dragonstone, Robert decided, since Summerhall was in ruins. It was
as good a choice as it could be; four days of careful sailing away from King’s Landing. And
not all the court needed to even remain there; plenty of Crownsland lords and ladies and their
retinue were only around to be seen and partake of Red Keep entertainments and hospitality
and not for the purposes of work. They could disperse back to their holdings, to reduce costs.
And if they did not understand the limits of the island’s purse, he was sure that Selyse would
find some way of gently, firmly, showing them all out of the harbor. Either that or Stannis
would just… grind his teeth at them, ruin their fun, and they’d be fleeing for their collective
health.

Other governmental functions such as the Small Claims Court would continue on within
King’s Landing, held in temporary offices, set up in various buildings that were confiscated
Targaryen loyalist properties, now claimed by the Crown or rented from families such as the
Florents, at reasonable rates.

Just about the only person not evacuating the Red Keep was Maester Pycelle; his only duty
during this time would be to attend to the Ravenry and it was expected that a multitude of
birds would be flying back and forth from Dragonstone, to maintain continuity of
governance.

It was all planned out very well by the Florents and Jon Arryn, even down to the schedule of
boarding the ships to Dragonstone.
Just about the only intractable obstacle was Cersei, and everybody expected that.

“You know she’s going to complain about the island's sulfur fumes,” Stannis mentioned.

“We’re all going to complain about the island’s stink,” Robert chuckled. “Can’t be helped.
Any good hunting on Dragonstone?”

“There are mountain goats enough for the wild dragons to feed on, once upon a time,”
Stannis shrugged. “Perhaps you should take up fishing as well.”

Robert’s nose wrinkled at the thought of having to sit in one place, waiting for fish to bite.
Fishing was never half as exciting as a hunt.

“Are you very sure Dragonstone will do?” Stannis asked slowly, in the tone that the both of
them had learned was his effort at trying to not start a fight. “Targaryen pit?”

“... It’s just a castle. And I heard tell that you let Selyse take charge of renovations and clean
out.”

“I did.”

“So. Your wife has taste. And the money to indulge it. I think I shall remember it as more
your holding than anything else; she’s changed the place. I should like to visit it on that merit,
not just because it’s a place where I’m to continue doing work and duties.”

“Selyse has made many changes. She is not afraid to offer hospitality to a King.”

“Or a Queen, even one as Cersei,” Robert chuckled. “Well. It will be only for a few moons,
as the excavators are experienced from cleaning out the Dragonpit and the remaining
Alchemists don’t want to be shortened by a head. And remember, we’re not trapped on an
island with her, she’s trapped on an island with us! Hah!”



In the past years, Stannis and Selyse made visits to Dragonstone two weeks duration out of
every moon, to check in on Erren’s experiments and to maintain a connection to the
Dragonstone Islanders. When Stannis must address petitions from the banner Houses sworn
to Dragonstone, it was usually done at King’s Landing; it was much easier to resolve by
offloading onto the Small Claims Court if possible. Selyse, Delena, and Erren had years
enough to make changes to Dragonstone. Between the influx of cash that marrying Selyse
entailed and her and Erren’s efforts to increase income from Dragonstone holdings proper by
giving the small folk different sorts of work, the castle was transformed.

Dragonstone was the first to get glass from the factories in the Vale; Erren oversaw the
installation of proper windows by glaziers throughout the entire castle, sealed with caulking.
For the first time, the interior of the castle was more dry than damp. Carefully sited skylights
or clerestory windows were cut through stone, relieving as much gloominess as possible.
Selyse introduced gleam and glitter by having most of the existing tables and tops of cabinets
topped by glass, by replacing or replating all old candlesticks, candelabras, torchiers, and
chandeliers with brass, which caught and reflected the candlelight. As many rooms as
possible (especially the state rooms) had new stamped tin ceilings with angled panels and
patterns to further catch and reflect candlelight, an idea never seen before.

The innumerable dragon statues and bas reliefs that covered the stone walls were softened by
artisans who were charged with adding stylized brass or tin foliage and flowers from all over
the Seven Kingdoms, interspersed with the sly faces of foxes or does with fawns peeking out
at unexpected intervals from the plants. Since most of the columns of the castle were
decorated with coiled dragons already, it suited Selyse to commision stags as the new
decorative motif; torchieres were rearing stags holding a torch between their forelimbs, with
the prongs of their antlers supporting candlesticks along with new candelabras that were
brass stag heads, their antlers again supporting candles. It was here that the Lannisport
craftsmen tendency the gild the shit out of objects was allowed free rein in Selyse’s quest to
add more shine, as each sitting room, reading room, gathering room, and guest chambers all
had their own Lannister clock, topped with either a fox or a staghead. So many, in fact, that
they took on a new castle staff member dedicated to winding the clocks every day.

Oversized painting copies of a portrait tapestry of Lord Ormund Baratheon and Princess
Rhaelle Targaryen from Storm’s End were prominently displayed in the Great Hall’s largest
state dining chamber, the larger gathering chambers, the old throne room, and ballroom.
Stannis and Selyse posed for oil portraits, painted very capably by Delena, which were
displayed in the library and less formal gathering rooms. Within the ballroom, Erren’s
successful efforts at mirror-making was showcased; one wall was paneled with mirrors,
framed by brass in sharp Art Deco-esque style, quite in keeping with Dragonstone’s powerful
and hefty architecture.

For the rest of chambers less formal than the state rooms, Selyse went for what she privately
called Bordello Moulin Rouge Chic as a style. Different guest rooms were themed with
different colors, emphasizing the advances in dying and patternmaking of Florent cloth
holdings. It was entirely possible for any visiting House to be hosted in a chamber featuring
one of their House colors. Shiny Errenized cotton brocades and dyed fringe trims formed
curtains, upholstery, and bed covers. Clean white cotton sheets and lace-edged pillow covers
invited visitors to bed. Each bed had nightstands with scented candles within tin canisters.
Potpourris made from gathering and drying pine needles and rose petals of Aegon’s garden
were stuffed into sachets or even small pillows. Thick woolen Stormlands carpets covered the
floors for warmth underfoot. Landscape paintings were hung over the hearths. The dressing
rooms all had a mirror at a table, with an additional decorative box filled with good paper and
a simple black fountain pen.

Instead of old fashioned hard wooden chairs, proper leather wingback chairs and
Chesterfields or upholstered chaise lounges were available using a Florent brocade depicting
black stags leaping and galloping across cheerful yellow backgrounds. In the sitting rooms
and public reading rooms, she added tête-à-tête chairs to amuse and entice. There were felt-
topped gaming tables for cards and other table games with lighter cane-back upholstered
fauteuil chairs with gracefully curved legs. There were little brass wheeled tea carts and
inlaid wood cocktail cabinets. There were stacks of books with lighter, more amusing
subjects in ready reach on side tables.
Behind the scenes, Selyse ordered that the servants’ halls be expanded in width where
possible for ease of the servants going about their duties, that dumbwaiters be installed, that
wheeled carts be used for the ease of servants delivering meals and sundries and cleaning
staff delivering clean laundry. The kitchen made use of methane gas grills in addition to the
usual ovens and Selyse’s modern ideas on the efficiency and storage of kitchenware and
foodstock were implemented. Pantries, stockrooms, the stillroom, and wine cellar were
inventoried and reorganized, with all records updated.

The rooms were resort style before there was such a thing as a resort. It was stately, yet
inviting. The wet gloom of old Dragonstone transformed into something darkly seductive,
with leather, brocade, fringe, and mirrors. The visiting court exclaimed at the effect,
overwhelmed by the mood created and edited by Selyse. Even Stannis had not been fully
aware of all the cumulative changes instituted by Selyse. Renly pulled on his sleeve and
asked if he could make Storm’s End look like this when he was of age.

Stannis looked around, noting the changes to their private chambers while they rested before
preparing for the feast to welcome the royal court to Dragonstone. He leaned back, testing the
chaise lounge, while watching Selyse as she bathed.

“Everything is much more comfortable,” he finally said.

Selyse slowed her customarily rapid scrubbing with her washcloth and looked over her
shoulder at him, smiling.

“I am glad you approve.”

“I suppose everything is also, in some fashion, for sale?”

“Oh yes,” Selyse said. “I can see the envy in everybody’s eyes. King’s Landing woodworking
guilds have already been warned to prepare for an influx of new customers and I’ve had
Erren and Delena draw up furniture construction plans and instructions to pass on to them.
And Davos is very good at carving; he’s made miniature models of the new chairs and things
to go with the drawings.”

Stannis nodded. He could understand that; new markets for all the Florent fabrics for
upholstering, expansion of their assembly line techniques in the woodworking guilds would
greatly improve both quality and quantity of stock, lowering prices for good furniture pieces
and increasing trade availability into the houses of merchants and other wealthier
commoners, increased trade for either wool or cotton for stuffing, increasing the need for
what Selyse called tree farms; countryside smallfolk planting out and tending to carefully
chosen stocks of oak, maple, walnuts, ash and other trees, increasing the demand and trade in
lumber, new jobs all around, and all meaning higher sales taxes collected, to be put to good
use for all the improvements to King’s Landing and further on in the Seven Kingdoms.

The Florents’ tinkering resulted in the idea that just about anything could be powered by
treadmill or pedaling. For the Dragonstone kitchens, Erren put together a pedal-powered
blender that rendered ingredients down to pleasing smoothness for soups. Good, thick soup
was filling for the castle’s staff and if one can trust Selyse’s ideas of what she called nutrition,
the mix of ingredients rendered in a soup was better for a body than mere wheat or barley
flour baked into bread. Another blender was made that accommodated the quick rendering of
meat for making sausages or dumplings. Stannis could well see the use of such labor and
time saving devices for the making of masses of food, suitable for the canteens of both
marines or the Gold Cloaks. Selyse saw the potential in the manufacturing and selling of such
devices for the canteens that served shipyards, factories, public schools, or even the
charitable kitchens run by septs and motherhouses.

In the case of the visiting court, Selyse and Erren also used the same idea to design a pedal-
powered whisking mixer that whipped egg whites and cream, cake batter and egg yolk,
allowing Dragonstone’s kitchens to turn out desserts sure to impress with their lightness and
flavors. If Robert should be very impressed by it, the royal kitchens would get these blenders
and mixers along with recipes and from then on, nobles would be clamoring for their own, to
copy the cuisine enjoyed by the royal court. Selyse said that given the establishment of the
Seven Kingdoms Patent Office, Dragonstone would be exclusive manufacturers of said
blenders for twenty years directly, with Erren and Selyse co-owning the patents for that
duration.

Selyse was, in Stannis’ opinion, overly excited about yet another layer of governmental
bureaucracy. Granted, so far the only patents were for House Florent. He was told that Tyrion
was being encouraged to file for a patent for his clock design and for the Flushing Jake, to set
precedent and give the gloss of prestige to the new Patent Office. Selyse had explained that as
quietly as the Florents operated, the Lannisters under Tywin’s leadership did the opposite. It
would be good to let it be known that only Tyrion Lannister was allowed to go into business
building out his clocks and the Jakes. Would be copiers would be afraid of Tywin Lannister’s
wrath and facing any punishment he might take; he did not love his son, but he did love his
House’s name and good reputation.

Selyse slid down into the bath water soak, leaning her head against the edge.

“Stannis, take off your clothes and get in here.”

He undressed and got in. The tub was large enough for them to be comfortable side by side.
He scrubbed soap on before lowering himself to soak. They soaked in comfortable mutual
silence.

“All prepared for the feast?” Selyse finally asked. She lifted her foot out of the water and
brought it closer, checking to see how pruned she was. She put her foot back under; she
would sit for some more.

“Yes,” Stannis said. “We’ll show off Dragonstone’s kitchen skills and that we are finer
managers of the island than past Targaryens through the quality of the feast itself.”

It was a pity that the glasshouses were so very new; Selyse had surprised him by showing
him a collection of lemon and orange tree saplings, bought at great cost all the way from
Dorne, sailing to them in carefully tended pots as a gift.

They would simply make do with the cranberry sauce for the roast ducks. Stannis favored
sour above all other flavors. Robert could never understand it. Renly was also similarly
baffled, but he found Stannis' ability to take bites out of raw onions with nary a flinch the
way others might eat apples something interesting and downright awesome. There was some
twisted sort of pride shared quietly between Renly and himself about their willingness to eat
just about anything. They weren’t finicky or precious like other nobility. They knew what it
was to struggle. To starve. So they would occasionally notice each other staring too
contemplatively at pigeons or gulls in King’s Landing. And never saying a word about it.

As this was a feast that he was nominally holding, Stannis would have to be prepared for
gladhanding. Robert’s presence would always be helpful for drawing away the more tedious
or obnoxious of nobility, but he must display unflinching ability and impress those directly
sworn to him. At the least, House Velaryon and House Celtigar should be carefully cultivated
and any grievances against House Targaryen acknowledged and leveraged. Stannis slowly
exhaled before standing to climb out of the tub.

Selyse followed after and Stannis had a moment's thought that what would be really useful
for settling the mounting annoyance and distaste for the upcoming festivities would be an
orgasm. On the other hand, the new bed looked far too welcoming and he would never be late
to his own appointments if he could help it.

“Feeling down?” Selyse rubbed his shoulder.

“Yes.”

Selyse kissed his cheek.

“We may rest later. But tonight. We perform.”

Stannis nodded.

It was a ridiculous balancing act; they must appear rich, and yet not outshine Robert or
Cersei. For this, he had a new set of court clothes. The golden thread that formed the
embroidery was even more dense than before and heavy. Armor was one thing. This?
Absolute waste. Granted, Robert would be wearing his cloth of gold cloak, which was even
more unwieldy, in addition to his crown. So Stannis had relative freedom. Selyse echoed him
with black and gold velvets, a column of slinky fabric draped languidly over her hips, and
glittering at her shoulders were beaten gold sequin swirls forming abstracted antler rack
patterns, dusted with topaz and citrine beading, splashing across her back and down her long
sleeves to her elbows. Her neckline plunged low at the front, daringly so. The paleness of her
skin there was set off by the fabulous long five-strand pearl necklace she was wearing for
tonight, all Dragonstone pearls from the pearl farms Erren and the other Florents helped
establish.

She looked at herself in the mirror. She rolled her shoulders, throwing them back and lifting
her chin, becoming authoritative and serene, plastering on her placid Court Face. She turned
her head and the gold embellished topaz studded hair pins from her wedding glinted in her
hair.

“Into the fray, Stanny Blue Eyes.”

“Yes.”
They checked in on Armand. He was happily installed in the nursery and secure with his
toys.

She tucked her hand at his elbow and they headed out to the feasting hall.

They ate well on garlic bread, Florent onion soup, baked oysters, lobster tails, chicken
braised in wine, breaded white fish filets pan fried in butter, endive salad, lamb with mint
sauce, roast duck with cranberry sauce, hard and soft cheeses sliced thin and spread on
crackers, brisket with molasses baked beans, and finished with egg custard pies topped with
ostentatiously tall meringue caps.

Stannis managed as he had learned over time at King’s Landing; his handshakes were firm
yet not bonecrushing, he nodded in greeting (He did not smile. That was utterly beyond him
in the moment among near strangers and strangers) and made sure to say everybody’s name
in acknowledgement. He stated with some genuine feeling that he hoped the trip over was
fine, that nobody suffered too much from seasickness, and that their rooms within
Dragonstone were to their taste and comfortable. He accepted compliments about the feast
and Dragonstone itself. For this, he proudly repeated that it was Selyse’s doing. It was
simple, always, to give credit to her.

Selyse did her magic. She somehow, despite laughingly jesting in private about how tedious
some people she encountered were, managed to easily be welcoming, smiling occasionally
but not too widely, perpetually pleased to meet and greet and give compliments to all and
sundry.

“Lord Celtigar,” her tone was ever inviting. “How well you look this evening! What a fine
way to wear your hat!”

She then reached out and patted his forearm, saying that he looked very elegant in High
Valyrian.

“Did I get that right?” Selyse tilted her head with inquiry. “I trust that you would correct me,
if I made any mistakes at all?”

Aged Lord Ardrian Celtigar brightened from her asking for his advice and good opinion. His
riches were the labors of his ancestors and any prestige was outdone by the rival Velaryons.
To say nothing of looks; House Celtigar boasted the purple eyes and silver hair of Valyria
well enough, but they were not bred so fine in the bone nor fair in the face. It was entirely
possible for Valryian people to be plain and unfortunately, House Celtigar exemplified this.
To be noticed by the wife of his overlord was quite the compliment!

“Your accent is charming!” he replied also in High Valyrian. “You do your studies great
credit.”

He would stay longer, to make much of Lady Selyse’s fluency, but oh, Lord Velaryon had
overhead and now, as ever, he was being pushed aside by the more handsome, more charming
man who was all too eager to speak in their shared language together. He made his parting
bows and went back to his seat.
He only sat down for a little while, before a servant appeared, holding a note. He opened and
read it. It was in Lady Selyse’s hand, begging for forgiveness for her impertinence, but she
noticed that he had a cough and was hoping that he was not too put out by her offering him
some cough lozenges. The servant held out a dish of lozenges and Lord Ardrian took one. He
put it in his mouth, prepared for bitter herbals, but it was alright. Anise, sage, thyme,
peppermint, and horehound in a dried molasses mixture which worked to immediate soothing
effect.

“My thanks,” Lord Ardrian said. “I’ll have the whole dish in my chambers.”

The servant nodded and left and Lord Ardrian was more pleased than he had expected. How
gracious a lady, to care for guests so well, what hospitality!

Everybody rested after the feast, digesting. They had two days to do so before attending a
ball, the first ball on Dragonstone since last Targaryen possession. When the servants threw
open the double doors into the ballroom and everyone saw the wall of mirrors, they gasped.
Glances were made at the famously austere Stannis for his reaction to the undoubtedly costly
extravagance of his wife.

Selyse grinned at him and he raised her hand to his lips to kiss once. Simply that, nothing
else.

Astounding.

The Mirrored Ballroom, as Dragonstone’s ballroom was already being called, put to shade
the ambitions of all sorts of aspiring mistresses and their grasping fathers. What did she have
to do, to get something like that!? The whole of Dragonstone was to be her jewel, the
courtiers whispered, her own pleasure palace. Some like Prince Oberyn remembered how
Dragonstone was under the Targaryens and to see it transformed so; wondrous. Costly. Such a
woman, who could extract prodigious sums from a man as Stannis Baratheon must be more
beguiling than the best trained courtesans out of Lys.

It was all a bunch of ridiculous tosh, Lysa knew.

Lysa knew very well that copper and tin were pulled up in the tons from Royce mines for the
brass and tin jarring of the Royal Fleet and Iron Islands Trading Company and all the fabrics
within the castle must be Florent factory-made and paid at cost. It was not costly, so much as
time consuming to have all these goods made. But they did have years to do so, after all. It
was not Lord Stannis alone paying for Dragonstone’s changes, but Selyse’s own money and
her family money and family sources in addition. She knew that wonders came out of the
Foxhole and here, in Dragonstone. She didn't quite understand what was so wonderful about
the new Seven Kingdoms Patent Office when Selyse told her of it, only that it made Selyse
and other individual Florents rich off of their ideas. The idea of that was entirely new and
strange and she certainly could not have come up with it on her own. Jon wasn’t quite sure
himself of what it meant or the importance. Not even King Robert. Yet Selyse was convinced
that letting the acolytes, maesters, and other learned men of Old Town know of such a thing,
let alone the more creative amongst the crafting guilds would cause more innovation and
business to grow and increase within Westeros.
With all these courtiers here at Dragonstone, Erren was forced to leave his labs; he had to
assist Selyse and Stannis in playing host and to keep operational security by barring the way
into the most secret of areas; an entire wing of the older, more fortress like of Dragonstone
converted into workshops and labs. Lysa knew of them. But she certainly did not know where
or what went on inside them. She didn’t even know the entrance proper to the lab section of
Dragonstone. She would not be surprised if an entirely new false wall was built for the
purpose of hiding it and that you could only enter if you knew which fox statue to stand in
front of and-, she didn’t know, you pressed a paw or nose to open a secret entrance. She did
not care to know more; it was enough that House Arryn was benefitting with glass factories,
porcelain factories, and surely, mirror factories after all these lords and ladies got a good look
at the Mirrored Ballroom. Already, she could predict all the new, comfortable, frankly sexy
upholstered furniture would be all the rage and the Florents would reap more profits from the
furniture making guilds purchasing fabrics for upholstering.

The business of governing would continue, no doubt, but with Dragonstone so transformed, it
was a time for some well-earned leisure, she thought. Jon looked quite refreshed already, with
the last of the wildfire caches finally being cleared and his worries reduced. She was ready
for the ball wearing an Arryn heirloom piece; a silver necklace with sapphires as large as
quail eggs. Her draped column gown of shimmering Errenized cotton was also blue, with
silver embroidered falcon shapes at the collar border of her bodice. At her wrists were silver
cuffs, engraved with leaping trout on waves.

Queen Cersei shone golden in the candlelight of the Mirrored Ballroom. A ruby and gold
tiara fronted her traditional heavy crescent rolled and braided Westerlands coiffure and a
matching heavy gold necklace of rubies framed by diamonds glittered at her neck. Her gown
was made out of the new lion brocade that was so popular with the Lannisters these past
days. Her skirt was narrower as a concession to the popularity of the style set by Selyse and
herself, but flared out wider at the knees with heavy flouncing and her sleeves remained
flowing and dagged. She was pleased with herself, pleased by the splendor of her raiment,
pleased by looking at herself in the mirrors.

The Mirrored Ballroom was spectacular in candlelight. It seemed as if they were dancing on
forever, the mirrors creating an enchanted magical tableau. The punch bowls remained
topped off, the idea of having supper during the middle of the ball instead of eating
beforehand so that the dancers would not feel too heavy was quite clever, and having many
card tables and chairs at the perimeter for the comfort and entertainment of those who wished
to sit out was considerate. As usual, Jon danced with her for the first half prior to supper and
then sat out to rest for the second half, watching her fondly as she danced with others. She
hoped that Jon would live long enough for little Roland and Elyse to have fond memories of
their father; he was such a kindly husband. So important to the Realm; why Lord Stannis said
all the time that he couldn’t do half of what he accomplished with the Royal Fleet if it
weren’t for her husband supporting him!

She danced with Lord Renly and King Robert and any number of Florents and Valemen.
Selyse had warned her that as it was inevitable that she become a widow that she must be
careful about being seen to favor one man or another before her husband passed. She may do
what she wished afterwards; Selyse called it being a merry widow, but until then, she must
not risk Roland’s position. She was Lady of the Vale. She went to play rounds of Mere,
claiming victories, and went to sit with Lady Samantha Florent to exchange observations on
the ball. Lady Samantha was never so obvious as to be seen taking notes in public for Page
Six. Lysa thought she would simply have to write up on the Mirrored Ballroom. Yes, and the
newest style of… furnishings for the stately, gracious home. Smallfolk, no matter how
wealthy, didn’t have keeps, after all. She’ll have to ask around as to the opinions of others on
what they thought of their guest rooms afterwards. Quotations gave columns authenticity.

And as the finale to the ball, Erren Florent announced the newest in entertainments, a
spectacular, never before seen treat for all and sundry, an amusement to write home about!
They went outside to Erren’s showman patter and directed to look up into the night sky, over
the harbor.

The crowd settled and then Erren blew a horn.

All was quiet, then what Lysa could only describe as a streak of fire, whistled shrilly in the
night air as it rose up as fast as an arrow, high, high, high and then exploded into a- a flower
of yellow flame in the sky. The crowd gasped. It was not the wild sick green of Wildfire. The
crack and boom were not as terrifying as real thunder, but the flashes of light, it was similar
to lightning! They watched, entranced, a little frightened, while King Robert clapped and
cheered and hooted from each explosion in the sky.

“Extraordinary!” Jon leaned in to her. “What can they be? They don’t look like wildfire at
all!”

“Erren Florent would know!” Lysa replied. “Goodness, that one was big!”

They glanced at Erren, who was also looking up at the sky. A boom and his face was
illuminated. He had an eerie, mad look of joy on his face.

“Hmm,” Jon said.

“What is it?”

“... I expect that these are not mere entertainments.”

They watched as another series of explosions set off.

“... Weapons?” Lysa ventured after a few moments. “They are fire flying in the air.”

“Just so,” Jon nodded.

“They shan’t sell to just anybody,” Lysa said faithfully. “They’d know the risks.”

Jon hummed again. They watched all the way to the end of the show.

It really was some thing to write home about!
                  Chapter 46: Dragonstone: Vacationing


The following days were relaxed with easy amusements. Lysa went with groups of ladies
who found reason to rise early in the morn and peer out of certain windows, giggling at their
own daring, to watch the Marines’ daily training jog on the beach in their short sleeved shirts
and training short trousers, some bare chested. She would then have Roland and Elyse sent in
from their nursery, and go to sit with Selyse, who now liked to write while Armand and his
nurse were in the room with her. While Roland and Elyse were carefully rolled onto their
tummies for Tummy Time, Armand would play by himself, still too young to take notice of
the two new babies in the room. Lysa hoped they would grow to be best of friends. And
perhaps more? She was sure that Stannis and Selyse would not take issue to the idea of a
betrothal between Armand and Elyse, but Lysa was learning that they would much prefer
later arrangements, as was done for the main line Florent cousins and Selyse herself. Persons
should grow and have known characters before being made to do their duty to their Houses
by taking on the responsibility of marriage.

She supposed it made much sense; Catelyn was completely insufferable at twelve, going on
and on about her great match with Brandon Stark. What little girl child of twelve knew what
marriage truly was? And truly, why should she be so eager to let her daughter go? There was
no telling if they should be blessed with another sibling and if they were the only two Arryns
of their generation, how more precious they were! Roland’s match would necessarily be of
great consideration. But Elyse, Lysa thought to herself, running her fingers through her little
girl’s strawberry blonde hair, she could wait. She ought to be courted by suitors and have her
heart’s desire. A time of peace and no risk of being tied to a husband many years older than
her. This was Lysa’s burden and she would not have such a thing happen to her own daughter.

Selyse would practice her instruments and sing, or both of them would read and write with
Lady Samantha. Delena would join them or not; she would often be found sketching various
scenes of Dragonstone and painting. Various ladies would drop by for tea and table games or
sewing. The comfort and ease of Dragonstone was such that even the necessary duty of
paying visits to Queen Cersei was not such an ordeal that it usually was. It did help that she
was much occupied with Prince Eddard.

Prince Joffrey was not used to his mother attending to anybody else. He was seasick the
whole trip over, frightened by the uncontrolled rocking of the ship, and the unfamiliar
surroundings. He tried clinging to Cersei, only she was not any better when it came to
seasickness and they drove each other apart with the smells. He miserably wanted Robert,
except Robert was on an entirely other ship. Selyse had delicately advised Robert on the
sense of separating the Royal Family for a ship journey. He saw the sense of it; the deaths of
his parents was a sensitive subject, but he was going to learn better from it.

He was fussy and unhappy with all the changes and an unfamiliar nursery and bed. Stannis
took the time to tell him some Florent childrens’ stories, attempting to distract him. One
quickly became his favorite, one that Stannis was ordered to tell again and again.
“-The Gingerbread Man ran and ran deeper into the woods until he saw a hunting hound. And
the Gingerbread Man said, Run, run as fast as you can-”

One day, Joffrey was so sick of Mother and the stupid baby, who wasn’t interesting at all!

Selyse of course wanted to go on walks while on Dragonstone and Lysa was convinced into
descending down into Dragonstone’s fishing town. Lysa never had much to do with smallfolk
before. Certainly, she was taught a condescending graciousness in manner when it came to
addressing smallfolk who entered Riverrun during petitions to Lord Hoster. It was barely
acceptable in terms of her natural shyness. It was only after getting to know the Florent ladies
and learning to hold gatherings and dinners with Kings Landing’s merchants and
guildmasters that she eased into understanding the need to converse with sincerity with
commoners. Riverrun certainly could not have prepared her for it; other lords had towns and
more experience speaking to the more educated and canny commoners. The business of
ruling a city caused one to have more than lords and ladies, knights, and men-at-arms that
needed consideration. Lysa was not taught to respect the qualities of merchants and the
professional smallfolk of trades.

Selyse demonstrated simple respect. She did not save her courtesies for the nobility. Very
occasionally, she would go out with escort into the markets, taking surveys of the spread of
Florent fabrics and other interests. She could while away time collecting gossip from
merchants and their wives, inquiring about any news from afar, taking note on the general
opinion of the Baratheon regime within King’s Landing.

Selyse was gregarious as she always was, being a gracious Lady of Dragonstone, holding
informal conversations instead of petitions with the people. One method of avoiding the
necessity of attending to Queen Cersei was to have these conversations as afternoon teas,
outside of the castle itself. One of the nicer inns would set aside a table for her and her
guests. Selyse found that Erren was well-liked and that the castellan of Dragonstone was also
seen as fair and worthy. The biogas digesters were maintained in good order and the stationed
Royal Marines caused no undue troubles. The armory had a healthy stock of dragonglass
arrowheads and crossbow bolts, along with knives. The dragonglass knappers continued to
labor on and were paid well for their work.

Lysa supposed it was a form of economy; the imported steel that might have been turned into
arrowheads or bolts would be saved for other weapons and armor. With Dragonstone’s unique
stores of this natural resource, it made sense. Lysa was unaware of the finished arrowheads,
bolts, and daggers being sent onward in bulk to Eastwatch.

There were more secluded beach coves where the ladies could lift their skirts and shed their
stockings to wade into the waters. It was cold! Colder than Riverrun’s friendlier waters and
Selyse said the same; Brightwater’s waters were warmer than the sea. They discovered that
they both learned how to swim as children and it was quickly decided that they should both
like to go swimming. Selyse and Lysa designed with Delena some swimming clothes to sew
up. Lysa would die of embarrassment should any man witness what they came up with, but
acknowledged that skirts were dangerous for swimming and would cling when damp anyway.
They came up with black short-sleeved one-piece singlets that ended just below the knee that
buttoned on the front. To this they added quickly drying cotton slip-on shoes with cork soles.
They would cover themselves with cloaks and broad hats to walk down to the cove. They
swam out and it was bracing to float and drift, laughing as the waves hit them.

Eventually, notwithstanding her embarrassment, it was known that a group of ladies were in
the habit of swimming at a certain cove. Lady Samantha and other dowagers slyly let it be
known that Lord Stannis was just about pulling his visibly sparser hair out issuing
punishments to offending men who foolhardily got caught climbing the bluffs to spy upon
them. Lysa was sure her face was unattractively blotchy from the mortification. Selyse of
course did not feel embarrassed one way or another and went to comfort her husband on the
matter and to come up with a solution.

Said solution was to have Stannis himself accompany them while swimming. Lysa could just
about kill Selyse for this!

Yet it was sound; absolutely nobody wanted to get caught looking upon the Lord of
Dragonstone himself in dishabille. And he certainly would not look at the women; he was so
proper! They sewed a swimming singlet for him also and the first time he marched, scowling,
alongside them to the cove, Lysa had to stifle her nervous giggling. Selyse tried to lighten the
mood with some small talk on the way, but Lord Stannis was not having any of it; he was
harumphing the whole way down. Selyse shrugged and entered the water after dropping her
cloak and towel. Lysa quickly did so as well as the other ladies. Stannis was courteous; he
stood with his arms crossed, facing away from them, glaring at the bluffs, as if daring
anybody else to look upon them.

They swam, until they were ready to go back ashore.

“Your turn, Stannis,” Selyse called out, wrapping her towel around her shoulders.

“It’s not necessary.”

“Look, I sewed that for you, you’re getting it wet. Please?”

Does he even know how to swim? Lysa thought to herself, consciously avoiding looking at
his bare biceps as he scowled at Selyse.

There was a moment of teeth grinding and then Stannis strode into the water, again as if he
was marching into battle.

“Hopefully he isn’t going to be stubborn and literally make it wet and come right back,”

Lord Stannis was cooperative and he dunked under and kicked, disappearing from view for a

They waited for him, making desultory conversation until Selyse stopped completely, with a

“Enough with the eyefucking, Selyse,” Delena drawled. “We’re in public.”

After that, more swimming singlets were made for the men who wished, even the King, so
that they could go to a different cove to partake of the sea. Omer and Merrell patiently taught
Sam how to swim; Renly knew how already. Sam was frightened at the prospect, considering
that his own father thought simply throwing him into a pond would force him into swimming.
His friends were much more sensible; he waded out, holding their hands, and they
encouraged him to crouch down, at his own pace, to submerge his face in the water while
holding his breath. After that they worked on getting him comfortable with floating.
Eventually, holding onto a cork life preserver ring, he learned how to kick.

The success of this method meant that Robert worked very hard to convince Queen Cersei to
allow them to teach Prince Joffrey. He splashed about wearing a cork float jacket at first for
even more additional safety, gradually learning. Otherwise, Joffrey was very happy to be
allowed outside, to be in the company of his father and uncles and the boys, and all in all
pleased to be away from his boring Mother. He learned how to make sand castles and spent
more time than expected patiently shaping walls and towers. He followed after the youngest
Florents and Sam as they explored the tide pools, investigating the sealife temporarily
trapped within view and reach.

The trip to Dragonstone got even better, by Joffrey’s estimation, from an especial camping
trip with his father and uncles and just him only! Well. Sandor Cleglane was also on the trip
and Ser Barristan and Ser Preston as duty dictated. But he did not care! Cersei tried to
dissuade him with tales about how wretchedly uncomfortable camping was and sneering at
the idea of sleeping beneath a tent on a bedroll and not on a soft featherbed. Robert wisely
told Joffrey that he would have the opportunity to piss on trees in the wilderness and he
would not need to take baths the whole time. Joffrey was sold on that! And anyway, he
declared, he was an entire five namedays old and plenty strong enough to go wherever his
father wanted him to go!



Erren during his mineral prospecting trips crisscrossing the island had refined the maps of
Dragonstone, taking into account goat trails and sources of water. He had a suitable campsite
set up in anticipation of the King’s visit, one a goodly ten or so miles out into the wilderness,
that would serve very well as a base for hunting from. It would be no trouble at all to get to
by horseback.

Robert had other ideas. He wanted to take a leisurely survey of the potential hunting
opportunities and would not risk a horse going lame on the trails when he was not familiar at
all. The island was safe; the dragons were gone and not a bear nor shadowcat lived on the
island. The mountain goats were preyed on instead by eagles and treecats. Treecats may
prove interesting, elusive quarry; the spotted cats were shy, evening or nighttime hunters
commonly only leaving tracks and feces behind as bare signs of their presence. Imry had not
seen a live one yet, just evidence of their kills from scattered mountain goat bones, hooves,
and horns. He recorded evidence in the form of teeth marks from gnawing and occasional
tracks, which he sketched.

Cersei screeched about the treecats. Robert thought she was overreacting; yes, a treecat was
larger than a five nameday old child, but on the other hand, he was going to be there, Sandor
was going to be there, and those cats were not aggressive at all, not like shadowcats. You had
to corner them in their lairs or chase them up a tree with hounds for the purpose. Treecats
were not known at all to attempt eating humans. He’d worry more about wild boar (not that
there were any on the island at all) in terms of sheer aggression.

They would hike, with packs upon their backs, Robert decided. They would set up camp at
the campsite Imry indicated on a map made for the purpose and spend time doing day hikes,
to get to know the lay of the land. Stannis thought it wasn’t unreasonable; he could do with
more familiarity with his holdings. Renly had never camped in this manner before and was
game, though a little concerned about the lack of comforts.

The tents in question would be small, enough to fit a single person lying down and everyone
would carry their own waxed canvas tent. They would have hiking sticks, tent pegs, and
cordage suitable for pitching their tents. Only Joffrey would be expected to carry only his
clothing and a portion of food in his pack. He was entranced by having a pack (just like
Father’s!) and opportunity to share Robert’s tent at night. They were provisioned with filled
waterskins, bags of dry beans, whole carrots, garlic, and onions, and oats and dried sausage
for cooking, and a mixture of crushed dried meat mashed with tallow, oats, nuts, and dried
cranberries that would keep for long distance day hikes, and bags of mixed nuts and dried
cranberries for quick bites as they hiked.

Cersei was still nervous, frightened by the idea of Joffrey innocently wandering away from
the camp and becoming irretrievably lost in the wilderness. Or perhaps he should fall down a
ravine! Erren had a whistle made for Joffrey, so that if he should get lost he would not lose
his voice futilely screaming for help. Other whistles were made and they practiced at blowing
on them, to make three short tweets, three long, and three short in succession for signaling.
He was told very firmly by Robert not to get out of sight on the trail and if he did, to stop
moving and wait. He would be taught more woodcraft out in the woods, once the camping
began, later. Joffrey could hardly wait.

Stannis had some misgivings about the ability of the pampered boy to keep up. Selyse
shrugged at that; they were a group of strong men, after all. If Joffrey did end up exhausted
and tantruming on the trail he was still small enough to be carried. Stannis grimaced. He’d
rather Selyse herself go on a camping trip; he had no doubt that she would travel at
acceptable speed, be clearheaded and cheerful on the march, and otherwise be an ideal travel
companion. Selyse kissed him and promised that she was willing herself. Stannis was entirely
gratified by her happy attitude about outdoor activities, considering Cersei’s loud
protestations against and Joffrey’s shrieking arguments to let him go.

They set off very early in the morning, with Joffrey stuffed full by Cersei with bacon and
eggs and a cup of warm milk.
They went at a slower than usual pace, careful to keep Joffrey in sight. He had bursts of
energy and excitement, wanting run run run when the mood took him. He was awed by the
sight of a lizard sunning itself on the rocks and picked up pinecones that had fallen on the
trail. He whacked at passing shrubbery with his hiking stick. He pointed at passing eagles
soaring overhead. He occasionally tripped on the uneven dirt of the trail, sprawling out
alarmingly with his whole body, but got up after an initial cry and sniffling, unwilling to
seem weak in front of everybody. As he wiped at the sweat growing on his brow, his face
became smudged with dirt. He was grinning.

He did tire as the trail began to gain in elevation, but they were in good time. He would be
encouraged to have some nuts and berries in order to keep up, to sip at his waterskin, and to
check if he felt like needing to potty. The first time, Robert led him off trail to a tree and
Joffrey laughed gleefully as he aimed at it, feeling very naughty indeed, just as promised.
They had not made it to the campsite by high noon, but they stopped to rest alongside the
trail, to eat a lunch of the dried meat-in-tallow chunk. Joffrey wrinkled his nose from the
smell of it and made a face at the taste, but chewed and swallowed because Robert took big
bites and dared him to. The group each had a single fresh apple for that day for lunch and
then no more fresh fruit left on the trip.

Joffrey surprised everyone by applying his stubbornness to the rest of the hike; though
refreshed by the lunch and rest, he had much less energy in the afternoon. He trudged along,
frowning in a determined manner.

“Do you want to be carried?” Robert asked.

“I can do it!” Joffrey puffed. “I can do it Father!”

But he was done and could go on no more; finally, he was forced to stop and dropped, rolling

Renly snorted a laugh. Stannis sighed.

“Well, that’s too bad. Guess Eddard’s the new crown prince, eh?” Robert stopped beside him,

Joffrey was too tired to say anything else. He made a half-hearted whimper instead and

“Well, at least we prepared for this,” Robert took off his pack and opened it. “We’ll get to

Robert took out a cloth sling big enough to hold Joffrey. He put it on, closed up his pack and

Selyse had in the past encouraged Erren to consider beauty in addition to the utility in the
selection and preparation of a campsite as a base for future hunting trips. She was wise, in
that there was a waterfall that emptied into a small fresh pool of clear water close by and the
pool fed an everflowing stream down the mountainside. The hiking party would be rewarded
by this view before making their way to the campsite upstream from the waterfall.

Once there, they would find that the campsite was prepared with a stone-lined firepit with an
iron grill placed nearby, and a pile of kindling. They set their packs down and made ready for
their first lunch. Robert took Joffrey out of the sling and set him sitting down upon his pack.
Joffrey watched, fascinated, as Robert made the fire with a flint striker and tinder and nursed
the flame, puffing away steadily with his breath, kneeling on the ground with his head low.
Joffrey had never seen his father in such a seemingly humble position. Yet it was necessary!
Robert stayed tending the fire. Stannis and Renly were pacing the clearing, determining
where they would like to pitch their tents. Sandor had taken the cooking pot and bucket, to
fill with water. Ser Barristan and Ser Prestan were standing guard.

After sitting quietly for some more, Joffrey felt strong enough and went over to Stannis and
Renly, who were working together on the first tent. Renly explained to Joffrey that a healthy
tree with no dangerous dead branches they could see was especially useful for pitching a tent.
One had to avoid the chance of a falling branch. One hiking stick was stuck firmly into the
dirt, an adequate distance away from a tree trunk. Renly showed Joffrey the knots used to
have the cord tied to the tree trunk already and Renly was holding the hiking stick upright
while Stannis secured the cord to the top of the stick. From there, the hiking stick kept the
cord taut as they secured the end to the dirt with a tent peg. The rectangular canvas was
arranged over the cord, down the middle lengthwise. The free ends of the canvas were folded
under and arranged to separate the bedroll from the ground directly. There were loops sewn at
regular intervals all around the hem of the canvas and four were chosen to be secured with
more tent pegs to tighten the whole canvas into a simple a-line arrangement.

“And that’s all?” Joffrey asked.

“That’s all.”

Joffrey knelt down and crawled into the tent.

“Mother would not like this at all!” he announced gleefully as he crawled out the other side.

He watched as Renly and Stannis set about pitching the rest of the tents. Renly had found a
pair of trees that had grown a satisfactory distance from each other and was thus able to
stretch the central cord between the two of them, not needing the assistance of any of his
hiking sticks. They next set up Robert and Joffrey’s tent. Sandor, Barristan, and Preston’s
tents were arranged in a triangular formation around the campsite, serving as perimeter
protection.

During that interval, Sandor had returned with water in the pot and bucket. Barristan and
Robert (Sandor would not approach the fire), moved the iron grill stand in position over the
firepit. The pot of water was set to boil.

Joffrey returned to the fire, curious.
“What are we going to eat?” he asked.

“Stew,” Robert said. “Beans and Roots.”

Joffrey’s nose crinkled.

“That’s all?”

“It’s camping. You’ll notice there’s not a pantry nor kitchen out here,” Robert waved at the

Joffrey looked at his little tin camping bowl, spork, and cup.

“Very well,” Joffrey finally said. “I want to go explore. May I?”

“Don’t run too far. And if Sandor tells you to stop and go to him, you do so immediately, you

Joffrey nodded impatiently. Robert looked at Sandor, who bowed his head. They walked off

Robert got up, satisfied that the fire did not need his full attention. Stannis and Renly

“It’s a good campsite,” Renly said. “Erren chose well.”

“Yes,” Robert agreed. “It’s good to be out in the wilderness, again. On a mountainside.”

“Regretting not bringing a proper hunting party?” Stannis asked.

“A little bit!” Robert grinned. “But I have time enough for that. Now, let’s get all the food
together and chopped.”

They had packed a wooden cutting board. Stannis and Renly set to peeling the carrots, garlic
cloves, and the single onion for that evening. They still needed to wait on the water to boil

Sandor had wisely kept him on the path towards the stream and they found a sandy spot after
clambering over water washed stones and cobble and found Joffrey throwing pebbles into the
water. Robert joined him, advising him on finding flatter stones and awed Joffrey by making

into the water trying to copy him. He succeeded in making a rock skip twice and shrieked
with excitement.

The sun was beginning to set by the time they made their way back to the campsite; Joffrey
was yawning and Robert was carrying him on his back.
Stannis and Renly were staring at the stew, with Stannis stirring it occasionally, lifting up the
ladle and the both of them judgmentally examining the thickness of the liquid.

“Any good?” Robert cheerfully called out.

Stannis cautiously tasted the stew.

“The beans are softened,” he replied. “It’s hot.”

Robert huffed to himself; that was not a useful answer in his opinion. But that was just
Stannis’ way. They waited for Barristan and Preston to unfasten their shorter white traveling
cloaks and to use wooden clothespins to secure them to a line of cord stretched between trees
to form a clothesline for the purpose of keeping the cloaks clean before returning to find seats
on the ground. Joffrey was amazed by the idea of sitting directly on the ground. The stew was
ladled out.

Perhaps it might have been bettered with salt or dried herbs; they had not taken any, this
being the first sort of camping they attempted. But it was hot and filling and after a day of
hiking, Joffrey had no complaints and hunger made everything delicious. Sandor took the
empty pot back to the stream to rinse out and then to fill up again and set it to boil over the
fire, to sanitize the water for tomorrow. Afterward, they sat in silence, staring at the dancing
fire flames, all the men not moved to say anything. Eventually Joffrey slipped sideways and
fell right asleep in the dirt, dead tired. Robert lifted him up and took him to their tent, took off
Joffrey’s boots and dirty socks and day clothes, put him into a nightshirt and tucked him into
a woolen quilt on top of his bedroll.

Robert quietly returned to the fire.

Talk lazily rose up then. It was decided that for future camping, perhaps they could have
Dragonstone carpenters sent up beforehand to build some simple benches and a table; Stannis
and Renly had to chop up the vegetables with the cutting board on the ground and Renly was
finicky about the vegetables so close to the dirt. Robert said that what would really liven up
proceedings would be a cask of ale.

“Then you must carry it up here yourself,” Renly said. “For I shall not hike with a pound
more than required!”

Sandor snorted, but said nothing; he and the Kingsguard hiked up wearing plate armor.
Admittedly, they were offered the option of lighter leather armor given the safety of
Dragonstone, but it was the principle of the thing. They were on duty on this trip.

“We do need a barrel or box, though,” Stannis said. “There is no place to easily secure our
remaining food from animal theft.”

They had collected all of the food together into a single sack and then tied it shut and had a
rope tied around it. At the other end of the rope they tied a rock and flung the rock and rope
over a tree branch (which took some walking around to find one that wasn’t too high) to pull
the sack up off the ground above their heads. The rope was then tied around the trunk of the
tree. The sack dangled in midair out of reach from theft by foxes or ground rodents and
hopefully not an intriguing target for inquisitive island ravens and crows or squirrels.

“Now that’s a practical idea,” Robert nodded. “Make note of it.”

Stannis had his notebook out already.

Further plans for improvements were made, before they lit their candles within their folding

Joffrey was still sleeping in the morning after sunrise. The cacophony of woodland birds
finally woke him and he sat up, a little confused at finding himself inside the tent, before
throwing himself upon Robert’s gut. Robert grunted in surprise.

“Eh! Eh?”

“Get up!” Joffrey cried. “What are we going to do today? Huh? Huh, Father? Get up!”

Robert chuckled and they untangled themselves from the blankets and crawled out. Joffrey
wiggled his bare toes in the dirt, having suddenly learned not to step too hard on the
pineneedle covered ground. Robert stretched and yawned and Joffrey did the same, rubbing
his eyes. Joffrey shivered a little in the morning air, thrilled at the strangeness of being
outdoors wearing his nightshirt.

“Did you sleep well?” Robert asked.

Joffrey wanted to say no; it was not at all like sleeping on a featherbed. But, he was here with
his Father and he had so much fun so-

“Yes!”

“Very well. Breakfast after dressing and brushing your teeth. And then we hike!”

After a breakfast of oatmeal with dried cranberries and slices of dried sausage, they refilled
their waterskins with boiled water and portioned out the meat-in-tallow along with trail mix.
They set off as a group, following a route recommended by Erren’s map, which Stannis was
in charge of. Robert talked freely to Renly and Joffrey, a running, surprisingly educational
flow of words about his observations about prevailing wind and how that would affect
stalking prey, noting locations of established game trails, noting any creeks and water sources
they passed which would attract wildlife, pointing out the subtle changes in vegetation in
relation to elevation and wind exposure, and comparing with what they were experiencing to
what he remembered from the mountainous terrain of the Vale. At high noon, they would
stop and eat lunch and consult the map. Erren’s routes were all loops back to the campsite. It
would be decided then whether or not they should press forward as a whole group or whether
or not Sandor should double back with Joffrey while everybody else pressed forward to meet
at the campsite later.
They were very lucky that they did spot a white mountain goat, a mature billy, walking along
a ridgeline one day. Robert pssped, going quickly into a crouch and waved his hand behind
him. Everybody followed suit.

“Joffrey! Joffrey, look!” he whispered excitedly. “Look at the size of him!”

“Oh!”

They watched.

“If you had your bow, what would you do?” Joffrey excitedly asked.

“Check the wind,” Robert replied. “Check your shadow. You’d want to be higher than the
goat, ideally. So you begin the stalk. Don’t want it seeing you and running off. Go off trail,
keep upwind, maybe have to stop and wait if it happens to look towards you. Pretend to be a
rock. And if you get close enough, if you have it right, take your shot.”

“Oh,” Joffrey said, wide-eyed.

“If you get a good hit,” Robert continued. “If you get it right in the body, the soft bits, lung,
liver, gut, the creature will run off. They all will. So you must keep it in sight. Many hunters
lose their quarry in deep brush. It will run for… oh, near fifty yards, perhaps, if it’s a strong
one. You must follow and wait. Wait for it to die. Because even plant-eaters will fight to the
last.”

The goat passed out of sight and Robert began a crouched, fast stalk along the trail, trying to
keep it in sight. The others followed suit.

“If it dies and the body falls, it might slide downhill. It’s steep enough around here for it. And
then, the real work begins. The worst thing-”

Robert stopped. Everybody froze. Robert took off from the trail, uphill.

They crested the hill, scrambling, Joffrey hoisted up and clinging to Sandor’s waist, with
Robert going flat on the ground, waving his hand behind him, wanting the others to follow
suit. They did and carefully peered over the edge of the ridgeline.

The goat luckily did not run off. It was downhill, working its way along boulders and loose
rock.

“Like that,” Robert continued. “Shoot now and the animal will end up at the bottom. And the
worst thing is a hunter who rushes after the body. Look at the rock. See those piles of rubble
from past winter snows, carried down the hill? That’s treacherous footing. Don’t go right
after the animal. If it was dead down there, I’d go that way-”

Robert traced the air with his finger, pointing out a twisting, longer, yet safer route down into
the valley.

“To get to it. And then imagine. It wouldn’t be any trouble for me to haul one goat up by
myself. But anybody else, it’s a two man job.”
“Yes,” Renly breathed with understanding.

Joffrey nodded.

They watched as the goat moved out of sight. Robert blinked, his hunter’s intent passing
away. He stood up, holding onto his hat as the wind picked up.

“What a view!” he jubilantly roared and the wind carried his words away. “What a day!”

They all stood up and surveyed the view from the ridgeline; the wind pushing the clouds
along the horizon, the distant flat shine of the water of the sea, the line formed where the
elevation changed enough that even the hardiest of native pine trees ceased to grow and
instead low, prickly shrubs clung stubbornly to the cliffs, changing the color from dark green
and black-brown into mottled pale greys that contrasted starkly with the sharp, grey-black
rocks of Dragonstone Island itself. The wind was brisk, the insects buzzed, a far away bird
called out to mark its territory, and it smelled of brush, of sulfur, of distant salt from the sea.

They stood there, taking it in.

Robert reached out and gripped Joffrey’s shoulder.

By the time they returned to the castle, Joffrey had torn holes in both knees of his trousers,
his cheeks were smudged anew with dirt, he was reddened with the beginnings of sunburn, he
smelled of sweat, pine needles, and firesmoke, he was terribly hungry, and he was grinning
and shrieking with excitement. Cersei wrinkled her nose at his stink, as he babbled about
seeing a mountain goat.



Afterwards, various lords and knights trailed after King Robert as he hunted mountain goats,
once a sevenday, taking trips out that lasted three days at the most. Now familiar with the

foot within an hour of sunrise the next day. Robert, liking Renly’s idea of lighter packing and
from Stannis, speed of deploying, stressed that this was no leisurely hunt like in the
kingswood, with packs of dogs, gamekeepers, horns blowing, personal servants, and palatial
tents that required four or six servants to put up, with heavy central support poles. True, the
campsite was improved with a rustic table and benches and a food storage box and even
newly dug pit latrines, given the sudden influx of persons.

But this sort of camping and hunting was more rough, more primitive. More challenging.
And Robert did so like a challenge. He even pondered doing the same in the kingswood once
they got back to King’s Landing, stress testing more of the Florent methods and innovations
for camping and army equipping. As it was, Erren and assigned servants were fine with

on purpose, potential notice of the King or not.
Alekyne and Dacey, as well as Imry and the rest of the Florents arrived a couple weeks later

Jon Arryn had a fishing pole and net brought up, after Robert described the stream. He

By the end of the wildfire removal, Dragonstone’s new relaxing and romantic environs had

          Chapter 47: King's Landing: Best Laid Schemes


Alekyne and Imry made report to Selyse in the deepest part of Erren’s laboratory. It was a

They could safely stay overnights within Stannis’ office, where Stannis and Davos stashed

patience, and only when they were sure, could they make their entrapping pounce.

The administrative paperwork could safely stay in place to intimidate with sheer bulk; Royal

Maester Bryan clicked his tongue to himself in distaste at the state of the book shelf in front
of him. He had thought he would feel nostalgic and happy having a chance to go back

very energetically dusting the shelf on the end of the row, to speed up and duck out of sight.

Well.

He picked up a tome on Vale herbs. He walked some more and picked up a recipe book from
Dorne. He doubled back and picked up a book on turtles indigenous to the Riverlands. He
browsed slowly, circling, making sure that he was not tailed, as he was taught by Imry. Dear
boy. All of his Florent charges were so, so wonderful. He was blessed to have been assigned
to Brightwater Keep.

He was flipping through a tome recording old epics from the North, when he felt somebody
watching him.

“Yes?” he looked up.

A group of pimply Acolytes were hovering at the end of the row.

“Are you Maester Bryan? Of Brightwater Keep?” one of them whispered.

“I am,” Bryan added the book to his stack on a cart. “Why do you ask of me?”

“You wrote the treatise on cellular structures under microscopes,” one of them said in a
worshipful manner.

“You wrote the treatise that established the existence of the periodic table!”

“You wrote the treatise on establishing the validity of vaccinating for poxes!”

“Could you- could you sign my copy? Please?”

Bryan nodded and spent a few minutes signing the title pages of the proffered texts. They
asked questions and he answered them; it always warmed his heart when youngsters had
some appetite for learning. He made sure to mention that if they had any particular tomes
they wanted to be put into print, to write to Bellflower Press; the more popular texts where,
the more sense it would be to have them in print for easy purchase. Finally, the Acolytes had
to take their leaves. Bryan gave a friendly wave.

He waited for a few minutes before circling and doubling back on his route again. One of
them may be a spy, Imry’s advice came up in his mind again. Lose them. Avoid suspicion.

He picked up books. He put books back. He puttered. He hummed under his breath. He
genuinely straightened the books on a few shelves. His personal stack of books grew and
shrank as he pushed his cart along.

By the time the last bell rang to warn everybody that it was time for the library to lock down
for the night, he had the personal diaries of the High Septon during the waning years of Mad
King Aery’s reign in his lunch basket, easily hidden by a cloth and out of sight. He flowed in
the crowd of gray robed maesters and acolytes, pulling his hood up. He walked off, looping
and backtracking some more, until he reached his inn in Oldtown.

The security of the Library was appalling, Bryan thought to himself.

He packaged the diaries up with brown paper and string, to make ready for delivery to
Brightwater Keep.

He didn’t know why Selyse wanted the diaries of High Septon Maynard. He was not
supposed to know why and he accepted that he would be like a raven, unknowing of the
messages it carried, for good or ill. He trusted Selyse.

After this, he would be on his own for a few weeks to investigate the mood of the Citadel.
Perhaps debate some doubters of his and Selyse or the rest of the Florents’ work face to face.

taverns and pubs frequented by scholars and Maesters. Plenty were very skeptical about the

pudding; the Acclaimed has made over five successful voyages so far. So there. Women can

Rhea and Selyse together took the trouble to devise and publish proper mathematical

Renly knew well enough from discussion with Stannis that the potential of the flagship

good to have catapults if nothing was hit, after all.

After that, Renly began laboriously graphing out the arcs of hypothetical boulders from

Maester Willis reported that Lord Renly was working through his and Maester Cressen’s

Maester Bryan chuckled to himself. They were going to change the world in so many
