luckily one of the eldest and was afforded some respect from that.

She remembered how nervous she was, left by herself amongst these young lordlings and
ladies, who peppered her with questions at first about where she had come from and why
hadn’t they known of her before meeting her. She retold the story set up by the Florents; her
father was a Ser Girard Oldflowers, who fought in the War of the Ninepenny Kings. Before
leaving to fight, he traveled about, trying to earn some renown and coin at smaller local
tourneys. He’d made his way into the Westerlands and had met her mother, a daughter of
another knight. They fell in love and married there. He left for war and did not return and
Tysha had no memories of him. Her mother raised her until she died of consumption. Before
that could happen, her mother had managed to write a letter to Lord Oldflowers, hoping that
he would take Tysha in. She was ever so grateful, Tysha recited, for the generosity of Lord
Oldflowers in recognizing their kinship.

Some of the other children were doubtful, of course, though most took her at her word.
(Nevermind that according to Imry, the timing didn’t make sense. If she truely was a daughter
of a knight who died in the War of the Ninepenny Kings, she’d be older in age) It helped that
the Florents dressed her as soon as possible in Oldflowers colors; dresses of dark green and
jackets of white, trimmed in red piping and gifting her an enamel brooch, a circle of dark
green with a central white hand with a band of red crossing the palm that she always
remembered to wear everyday.

A Westerman mother explained all her own Westerman ways; the songs she knew were
different from the songs traditionally heard in the Reach. A daughter of a household knight,
respectable enough for a landless knight as the purported Ser Girard Oldflowers to marry for
love would not have been able to afford to teach her finer manners. Her ignorance of the
Reach was easily excused by her not knowing her father and keeping close to tend to an ill
mother.

She was desperate to learn and blend in and any missteps or low moods from her perceived
failures were brushed away as homesickness and grief over the death of her mother.

The Florents lied and lied and lied for Tysha.

She could not estimate how much of a debt she owed them. Maybe she could talk to Tyrion
about it, one day, and come to a reckoning.

She came to the door of Lord Alester’s solar and a Florent guard announced her. She was let
into the room.

“Ah, Tysha,” Lord Alester looked up from a ledger and gestured towards the more casual
sitting area with a low table and upholstered armchairs in the new style from Dragonstone.
“Sit, sit. Tisane?”

“Yes, thank you, my lord.”

She consciously lowered herself into the armchair with grace of movement, as taught by
Lady Melara, folding her hands neatly on her lap. Alester called for a fresh hot tisane and
joined her at the armchair opposite. When the tisane arrived, it came with sliced cheeses and
cold cut meats arranged on toasted bread and there was even an assortment of sweet pastries.
She nodded in thanks as Lord Alester filled her cup and placed a number of the snacks on a
plate for her.

Alester took a drink and looked at her expectantly.

“I wish to serve. I will swear an oath of service to Ser Colin.”

“You know your mind,” Alester smiled. “That is very good indeed. Explain your reasoning.“

Tysha explained over sips and bites of the snacks.

“You perceive and understand,” Alester concluded and smiled, this time showing his teeth
sharply. “Very good, very good! Yes. Yes, young Tysha. If it was not Tyrion Lannister, you
would have remained in obscurity. We had purpose not entirely charitable. It would not be
surprising if we earned no gratitude from you for it.”

“Ser Imry could not promise justice for me and Tyrion,” Tysha replied. “But he did promise
that House Florent would try. To do… what you could. And it seems that right now, with both
your brothers in good positions in King’s Landing, your children and niece married well, and
your House’s inventions and industries prospering, there is much that House Florent could
do. But carefully.”

“Yes, carefully. You do understand that what you may learn in the future, must first be
reported to Ser Colin and perhaps not even reported or hinted, to your husband?”
Tysha balked. She hesitated before finishing a sip from her cup.

“My lord? Even if there was clear and- and present danger to him?”

“In the direst of emergencies, I would not begrudge a loving wife’s actions,” Alester
conceded. “But if you should find out some conspiracy afoot amongst the gossip you gather
here in the Reach concerning the West, it is best that you report and Ser Colin find
collaborating accounts from his informants within the West. A single rumor is not fact.”

Tysha nodded.

“Now,” Alester stood up and went to his desk, where he opened a drawer and took out a
parchment document. “It is time. Read this, take it to heart. I will serve as witness to you
swearing service to Ser Colin in his duties as Master of Whisperers and the Seven Kingdoms
by oath, signature, and thumbprint. And then, we shall begin with new lessons for you that
will aid you in your duties.”



Willas Tyrell carefully gripped the inside handle of the wheelhouse’s door as he maneuvered
himself out of it. His sworn sword gripped the elbow of his left arm; it would not do to slip
and shame himself further by landing face first onto the ground. Once he had firm footing, he
leaned on his cane as he looked around.

Grandmother ordered him to see Bellflower Town for himself; Father would invariably
enrage her with the most shallow of observations and further duped by any hospitality offered
by Lord Florent in the form of good food and drink. As future Lord Paramount, she hissed to
him, he had to know the threat to their House’s position for himself. Not even depending
upon reports from various of their own household knights who were free to travel. With some
luck, he would be underestimated by that arrogant Lord Florent into thinking that Willas was
as… simple… as his father and not a threat at all as the heir.

Left unsaid was how Willas had learned the painful lesson that everybody was prone to
overlooking cripples.

Well. So he was a cripple. If he could use it to his advantage, then he shall.

Servants had been sent ahead of Willas’ retinue to seek out the best of the inns or the newer,
King’s Landing styled eateries for his refreshment. It gave him an excuse to linger and
investigate this culmination of Florent works.

The first signs that he saw himself were the boundary markers to Florent lands. It used to be
that one knew the border by twin stone foxes sitting upon tall pedestals, on either side of the
road. Here in the now, the Florents built up a single guard tower within view of the road that
also served as a signal tower. It would be expected, as a coastal Reacher House, that they had
signal towers along their coastal border. They expended funds and labor on their inland
approaches from the road that branched off the Roseroad. The tower was rounded with a long
mast rising up from the center holding the signaling arms. It was painted with blaring orange
and white horizontal stripes. Unmissable. As his wheelhouse approached, he could see the
arms moving, undoubtedly informing Lord Florent that he was on the road. When his retinue
stopped to water and feed their horses, he had the opportunity to stick his head out of the
wheelhouse window to look at the tower.

It had a crenelated roof and he could see bowmen looking down upon them. The lowermost
windows were traditional slit windows preventing easy entry by assailants. The upper
windows had wooden shutters that could be barred and glass (glass!) panes. The door to the
tower was iron-banded and undoubtedly reinforced well on the inside. A stone carving of a
fox’s head looked down upon the road from the capstone of the tower’s stone doorway. He
waited and asked for a report from the captain of his guard as they left. He had ordered the
tower guards to allow his men in for an inspection.

“There are horses at the ready kept at the stable,” the captain said. “It is their purpose to ride
out and alert the closest villages should this tower come under attack.”

“For evacuation?”

“And mustering,” the man looked concerned. “The tower has a floor dedicated as an armory.”

“Armory?”

“It is so, my lord. Scores of halberds. Furthermore, the stairs to the second floor are not
proper stone stairs but made out of wood and made so that they may draw it upwards by
cranks and counterweights to thwart entry if they wished. Another floor serves as a food store
with barrels of water and ale and stacks and stacks of canned supplies, hard cheese wheels,
and entire hams. I have visited holdfasts with keeps less well prepared than that mere signal
tower.”

As they made their way further into Florent lands, those orange and white striped towers
were visible in the horizon, situated where possible on the apex of hills away from the road;
most roads naturally followed valleys or level land where possible. The amount, height, and
spacing of the towers were such that Willas had to assume that each were fitted with far-eyes.
Willas kept count of each tower and the idea of the Florents having such means as to equip
their signal towers with far-eyes in addition to manning them with defensive guards was
daunting indeed.

The same could be said by the quality of the paved roads that branched off from the Roseroad
into Florent lands. Even now there were lords that did not wish to spare the expense or
workers to improve their holdings’ internal roads, depending instead on the paved (by order
of the King) Roseroad, the majority funded by Tyrell funds and built by Tyrell laborers.
Florent spared comparably no expense. The same with Lord Tarly. Between the two Houses,
they straddled the Roseroad and both could very quickly muster forces and have them
traveling at great speed indeed to their borders and cutting off any approach by opposition by
Roseroad.

The Redwyne and Hightower fleet would of course helm the Florents in by sea, but the
coastal signal towers would ensure that they could not be surprised. It is fortunate indeed that
the Florents had no proper harbor for war galleys. There were concerning reports, though,
that Lord Florent was renovating and expanding on a wharf that previously was only large
enough for local fishermen’s boats. Instead of engaging the services of Redwyne or
Hightower shipwrights, they chose to exercise their connections to the royal family and
commissioned a sailing ship from the Royal Shipyard in Wendwater, a ship modeled after the
Acclaim and her sisters. The so-called cause was to allow for more frequent visits to
Alekyne’s wife Dacey’s homeland of Bear Island. Grandmother scoffed heartily at that, to be
sure.

Building out the wharf to serve a ship even half the size of the Acclaim (suitable for family
travel) made it large enough for merchants’ cogs. They were going to attract merchants that
did not want to pay Old Town’s docking fees or gate tolls nor middlemen who shipped
Florent goods by barge down the Honeywine River. And why should Lord Florent go by half
measures? He would build out his wharf large enough for Iron Islands Trading Company
ships to dock. The better for loading up his wares.

As comparatively a small amount of forces the Florents could raise, Lord Tarly’s experienced
men at war and all their assorted allies by blood and business made them formidable indeed.
And Tyrells did not have the bloodthirstiness of the Lannisters or even the Starks to bring to
bear. And the Florents never, never gave any sign of being more contentious now than in the
past.

It was not the Reacher way. Willas thought that certainly this would matter more when it
came to how to maneuver Lord Florent than Grandmother’s nervous grumbling about the
Baratheon appetite for violence and vengeance. Father made a temporary mistake, that was
all. Surely, once Grandmother and Father determined who should be his wife (certainly
somebody who would bolster Tyrell martial power) and his brothers’ marriages things will
balance out once again in the Reach, with their House secure. Florent’s opportunities were all
played out with his own children now and his fool of a son wed for love an impoverished
Mormont! Surely the Florent problem would not last once Alekyne followed his father in
assuming lordship.

His leg pained him and he had to ride in his lightest-weight litter chair.

Here in the middle of town, Willas compared it to Oldtown and found it disconcertingly
showing very well in comparison indeed despite the small size.

The Florents chose the bank of the river as the site of their town. The paved road branched;
one would lead to Brightwater Keep itself while the other went onward to the town. One
passed the castle to get to town; with regular patrols by household knights it was clear that
bandits would find Bellflower Town a tough nut to crack. Along the river bank there were
numerous waterwheels, and Willas could not imagine that so many grain mills were needed.
It was strange.

The entire town was neatly laid out as only a town that was ordered into being by a careful
lord could be. Despite the ongoing construction he could see with different buildings, it was
attractive. The Freys, Willas thought, would recognize a fellow need for symmetry and
proportion. The central paved road led to the water itself and crossed the river by what looked
like a stone bridge (it wasn’t made out of stone at all, but concrete), one with a graceful
arching span. It had a roof that covered the whole thing, which would serve well to shelter
defending archers and crossbowmen in all weather. On either end of the bridge there were tall
guard towers. One had a bell tower, clearly for alerting the townspeople of danger and the
other was a signal tower, part of a series that would pass on messages from the coast.

There were docks for barges near the far side of the bridge; it was clear the Florents weren’t
going to miss a chance at collecting their own bridge tolls and docking fees, no matter how
insignificant the traffic. It made sense, as the sheer amount of buildings with waterwheels on
the townside shore made docking infeasible anyway. The shoreline was further protected by
walls between the buildings.

The town was arranged around a central plaza square and the formation of buildings and
streets were neat, straight, ordered. In the center of the plaza there was a fountain, made in
the three-basin style of KIng’s Landing’s renovated public fountains. There was a raised
circular central basin for a waterfall spill and in the middle of that an oversized bronze fox
statue reared on its hindlegs, a forepaw raised in playful greeting, its jaws parted in a joyful
grin. There were five-petaled bronze flowers sculpted to form a wreath worn around the fox’s
neck.

Adjacent to the fountain was a permanent covered marketplace building; shoppers and
merchants alike could be sheltered from inclement weather by a stand alone loggia that
would be familiar to a Dornish person. It was a graceful structure with square columns
supporting arches and a tiled roof. There were statue niches inset into the largest columns
holding up the loggia’s corners and one niche facing the plaza already had a marble statue of
Lord Alester. On the column’s other niche was a statue of Alekyne, depicted holding a pen
and a drafter’s straightedge tool. Another niche had… the lady in question was depicted with
an open book and pen in her hand. Who-? Willas limped his way over. The inscription at her
feet said this was a likeness of Selyse Baratheon. Strange. Why would Lord Florent honor his
niece so? A shield was carved to be leaning against her knee and it depicted the rearing stag
of Baratheon. Ah. Currying favor with her husband, no doubt. Sharing that column was
another niche around the corner. That lady was holding an abacus and pen. And she was Rhea
Royce, judging from the shield at her feet.

The loggia’s market itself explained the necessity of shielding from rain; the merchants' stalls
were a fantasy of fabrics in all the different colors one could imagine. Bolts and racks of the
stuff, bright and cheerful, plain and Errenized, narrow ribbons and wide yardages, in cotton
and wool, along with spools and spools of thread ranging from the finest Errenized cotton for
embroidery to the thickest wool suitable for knitting. It was wonderful. It was something to
envy, as Willas observed the coins changing hands.

Outside the loggia there were other market stalls that did not need such especial protection;
dry goods and smaller wares and foodstuffs.

The streets themselves were also different compared to any others he had ever known. Paved,
of course, four ox-carts wide such that should a driver pull to the side to stop for unloading,
for example, cart traffic would not be blocked. On either side of the street, extending from the
base of the buildings there were raised pavements with a curb that prevented the dung from
livestock and horses from getting kicked into the way of pedestrians. The people on foot
could walk on these raised… sidewalks, and not dirty themselves with muck. These
sidewalks were additionally wide enough for a group of four standing shoulder to shoulder to
pass comfortably. Every so often, Willas noted iron drain grates inset into the base of the
curbs, presumably to catch overflow from rains to prevent the streets from flooding.

Willas had not thought that so many buildings of a town not even ten years old could be made
of stone. The cost to buy quarried stone and to transport it; what expense! They were coated
in very smooth white lime plaster and had clay tiled roofs instead of reed or straw thatching
or wooden shingles. Grandmother Olenna was sure something underhanded was happening
when no reports of heavy ox-drawn carts of stone were observed going down the Roseroad.
(What Willas could not know was that almost all of the town’s buildings and the town walls
were actually built out of concrete cinder blocks, which accounted for ease and speed of
construction.)

Not only that, he would have expected there to be two-storied buildings at most. The central
plaza square was surrounded by buildings at four or five stories in height with shops at the
ground floors, expanding the opportunities for business. Many took advantage of the fabrics
available to have custom folding awnings affixed for shade or shedding rain from customers
walking by on foot. Building windows had wooden shutters and window rails painted in
blues or oranges, depending on taste. Some of the buildings were clearly residential;
balconies facing the plaza had lines of washing hanging out to dry and held pots of decorative
flowers or culinary herbs for personal use. There was a new sept on one side of the plaza that
looked to be made out of marble with stained glass windows! Across the plaza opposite, a
stately building that seemed with official purpose bustled with activity. There were Florent
guards posted. Willas had his guard captain inquire.

It was a town hall, a building of myriad uses. The large central room was such that it could be
used for feasting; once a moon the townspeople were treated to a community assembly where
sponsored local bakers, cooks, and brewers provided food and drink and any mummers
present were hired to play dances by the Florents. So regularly scheduled was this that the
more poor amongst the townspeople, rural smallfolk from surrounding villages, or even
Brightwater Keep’s staff planned for those days to be for their own personal celebrations.
Many frugal couples married on those community assembly days, where multiple couples
made merry procession to the sept, the septon cheerfully conducted their weddings, and then
the couples with family, friends, well wishers, and lucky bystanders filed into the town hall,
where they could feast and dance until the dawn of the next day.

To the sides of the hall there were rooms suitable for holding meetings between merchants
and guild members in conference and confidence. To the back there were offices of the tax
collector serving Lord Florent directly; more guards were posted. It was so necessarily well
guarded that money changers also set up there and traveling merchants with more precious
merchandise could store their goods or their money chests after a day of business for a fee.

The town was purpose-built to facilitate everything about the Florent fabric trade.

Willas was carried over to an eatery that he was assured catered to the most discerning of
visitors to town. Upon entry, he found himself in a dining hall as fine as a lord’s. The tables
had tablecloths, flatware, and cups were arranged as if ready for honored feast guests. Each
table held a small vase with fresh flowers. There were oil paintings adorning the clean white
plaster walls and the wooden floor was polished. Wealthier merchants, judging from their
clothes and some with prosperously plump bellies, sat quietly eating and drinking. No rowdy
inn was this! Willas was led to a table and the servant pulled back a chair for him.

“Shall my lord require me to read the day’s choice of fare?” the man softly, in the manner of
the most discreet and professional of servants, murmured. “Or will the lord read for himself?”

A man capable of reading, just for an eatery servant! Astounding!

“I will read,” Willas said, arranging the napkin (they offered napkins!) on his lap.

The servant bowed and offered a thick sheet of paper to Willas and retreated to a respectable
distance, where he stood at the ready.

Willas touched the paper and marveled at the printed text he saw there. Print, for an eatery!
Even at the better coaching stops and inns along the Roseroad, one expected the servers to
recite the day’s offerings.

Here, there were cooked meals; various meats seasoned with Reach-grown herbs. Tarragon
chicken. Chicken braised in red wine. Simmered duck with cherries. Local river fish pan-
fried in butter. If one wanted, they could have a meal with courses; Florent onion soup and a
salad, snails in honey and butter, a selection of cheeses and fresh fruit, and desserts of
custards, sweet tarts, or slice of pie. On offer were tisanes, tea, and wines both red and gold.
It was all in print, along with the prices. It was all very new, very different.

Willas raised his head and caught the eye of the server, who approached and stood at the
ready. He made his order and the man bowed, recited his order back and left with quiet
efficiency. He returned shortly to pour out wine and retreated again to attend to other guests.
Willas looked around and observed how the merchants conducted themselves. He was given
looks of recognition and curiosity; he was unmistakable with his cane and the gold and green
rose brocade of his jacket and the large golden rose cloakpin. But just as quickly, their eyes
lowered respectfully and they averted their gazes, not gawking like the lower orders of
smallfolk. These people knew about discretion. They had some sense of courtesy.

When the meal arrived, everything was set out very nicely indeed and Willas was left
comfortably alone. He ate and enjoyed the flavors more than he expected, given that this was
a public eatery. The cooks were good. Very good indeed. How strange it was, to eat so finely
at such an establishment instead of in some wealthy lord’s castle! How was this possible?

He inquired with the server and was told that the cook came trained from Brightwater Keep
itself; the Head Cook of the castle was hale and hearty and not likely to leave their position
and this ambitious cook was experienced enough to be willing to leave and take on the
business risk of opening their own establishment, with the blessing of the Florents.
Extraordinary.

Willas left the eatery after payment and ordered that his litter chair be carried at a most
leisurely pace in a circuit around the plaza. Time to explore.

He found a house of healing and midwifery; the corps of midwives and their apprenticing
assistants paid visits to various local villages on regular routes, dispensing care. As women
neared their time, they could even make use of a stable of ponies and quick, light wagons to
carry them into town; the signal towers were used to call for and direct the wagons.
Adjoining was an apothecary, where behind a counter there was an impressive wooden
cabinet of many little drawers and rows of shelves filled with mysterious jars filled with
ingredients that could help with a cough, reduce a fever, soothe aches and pains.

There was a public school for the children of the town and mill workers. There was a
daycare, where women mill workers could leave their babies and toddlers safely with
wetnurses and caregivers during the workday. There was an adult school, where after work
hours, workers could learn their letters and numbers in turn. There was a washerwoman’s
collective (not a guild, as there wasn’t truly some trade secret skill involved) that washed
workers' clothes and bed linens. There was a bathhouse. There were very many barrels for the
purpose of collecting stool and urine for composting or the use of the local dyers. The streets
were kept clean of livestock and horse dung with dung carters who collected the refuse for
composting. There were accountants' offices. There were law scholars; men of Oldtown who
had earned their link for Law at the minimum and were selling services to merchants for the
drafting of contracts.

There was a civil court, where issues between smallfolk could be addressed more quickly
than by audience with Lord Alester, using the advocacy of these same law scholars. Willas
was told that Lord Alester had found and hired on very learned law scholars away from
Oldtown, the ones that could prove with written testing records and recommendations from
the Archmaester of Law especially to serve as judges for issues such as a yeoman accusing a
neighbor of livestock theft or two merchant families disputing over the dispensation of a
daughter’s dowry in the form of coin or personal goods. The advocates would take up cases,
look up precedents, make arguments and then the judges would deliberate and dispense
judgements. Willas was skeptical of the idea, but apparently, smallfolk who did not agree
with outcomes could take it up with Lord Florent for an overruling, but the risk was that if
Lord Florent found that he did not disagree with the judge given good research and
casemaking, he would levy a fine for wasting his time at the least or worse.

Everybody seemed to agree that given Lord Florent’s even temper and generosity that to risk
“or worse” was the height of folly and much to be avoided.

There was a bookstore. Inside there were mostly printed books, though one could sell copies
in script and request a printed copy instead. There was even, and Willas could barely believe
it, a subscription library! Interested persons could pay a fee to cover the duration of a yearly
membership and enter a building with reading rooms and rows upon rows of books, where
they may read at their leisure. They couldn’t take books out of the building, but the sheer
generosity of the Florents was passing strange! To allow strangers to paw at books that they
must surely own!

In the evenings, after the merchants cleared out of the loggia market, mummers could set up
underneath and entertain the townsfolk with plays or music.

He found that Lord Florent had ordered household knights and more experienced men-at-
arms to train the men of Bellflower Town once a week at either archery or crossbow handling
and every other week the men of town had a training muster in a field outside of town where
they would train at halberds and marching maneuvers. There was a zealousness that Wilas
would have expected from Lord Tarly, not easygoing Lord Florent. It really was worrying.

But think, Willas thought to himself. Did it not make sense that Lord Florent would take such
precautions, given the commerce that was happening on his lands? The arming and training
of the city guards of Oldtown caused no concern for it was a city with a city charter and Lord
Hightower must needs defend his seat, his city, the Citadel, and the sea lanes. What could it
be besides foresight on the part of Lord Florent on behalf of his little town? Rumor and tales
would be carried elsewhere by the wagging tongues of merchants. The town was close
enough at three to four miles away from Brightwater Keep that a company of knights riding
hard could come to its aid in less than thirty minutes. Despite that, greed could push the
daring and violent.

This new town was a tempting target, no doubt. A large enough company of bandits who
scouted ahead of time would try to take the town hall, a grand prize holding the taxes
collected for the day and where the money changers and a few merchants kept their coins for
the day.

Waiting for them, however, was Bellflower Town’s defensive walls and bastions. They
enclosed what seemed like about a square mile (Ambitious! How many thousands did Florent
plan to pack into his town, to make it into a proper city!?) Two bastions flanked the town gate
and Willas wondered at their severely angular shapes as they approached. Could they be
like… fox ears? It could explain their shape. Willas noted the sheer number of arrow slits of
the bastions and the shadows of scorpions emplaced on top. The whole town was additionally
bounded by a wide defensive dry moat outside the walls; they had to cross a drawbridge.
Excess excavated dirt was formed into packed, also triangular mounds on the far side of the
moat, spaced such that they might funnel attackers towards where the bastions’ defenders
could rain down all manner of destruction from above. One such mound was placed in the
middle towards the approach to the town’s gate itself, preventing easy use of a battering ram.
It forced a split to the paved road going into town and with advance warning, Willas could
imagine waiting troops of archers on the mounds, good enough for defensive volleys before
being forced to retreat over the moat to stronger defensive positions behind the town walls.
Bellflower Town had its own armory and having the townsmen protect their town made
sense, to buy time along with the town’s guards.

And even getting past that formidable gate, there was that stretch of undeveloped land
standing between the town walls and the cluster of new buildings closer to the river banks.
They were being worked as farming fields for now. Open land, good enough for a last
defensive cavalry charge, to say nothing of a proper mustering of halberd wielding locals
trained in moving in step, standing firm against charging horses, and motivated to defend
themselves.

During the town’s planning, blocks of land lots were surveyed and set aside especially for
development by merchants as incentive to do business in Bellflower Town. Land leases for
the duration of 49 years (seven by seven, an auspicious amount) to be renegotiated afterwards
or sold on and a preferred discount for the use of cinder blocks and standardized architectural
plans for houses accounted for the uniformity. Richer merchants could see the benefit of
speculatively building out joined up townhouses on multiple lots leased, to rent out to
professional families who arrived later to town and wished for ready-for-move-in housing at
slightly higher rents to cover the original land lease and a little bit of additional profit for
themselves. And Lord Florent sat pretty, collecting total rents all the while from the 49-year-
lessees. Said funds were being pooled for the purpose of paying for town improvements and
services including the town wall.

Willas finished his friendly interrogation of the captain of the Bellflower Town guards and
turned around.

To face a smiling Lord Alester Florent, standing with an expectant air. Well. Not directly
behind him, his sworn swords would not have allowed that. But Willas was startled
nonetheless.

“Lord Willas,” Alester doffed his hat gracefully and swept a bow. “You honor me this day
with a visit to my humble little Bellflower Town!”

Willas graciously nodded back, scoffing to himself at the false modesty of Lord Alester
calling Bellflower Town little. Willas looked around quickly and saw that Lord Alester’s
horse was being held by his own pair of personal guards, far enough away for a measure of
discretion and no other retinue. He had ridden very quickly from Brightwater Keep to meet
with him. Willas was forced to concede that the signal tower of Bellflower Town was
annoyingly useful indeed.

“Well met,” Willas replied. “You have accomplished much in this place.”

“It was the work of many,” Alester replied and something about the acknowledgement of
others made Willas uneasy.

There was nothing for it. Willas straightened as much as he could and looked Alester square
in the eyes and said, with as much authority as a seventeen year old youth with not very
much practice could muster, that he would tour the mills of this town.

He had expected some measure of resistance from Lord Alester, some jealousy over the new
source of wealth to his house. But it was not so. WIthout changing his pleasant, faintly smug
expression (how his Grandmother loathed the man’s face!) Alester waited until Willas was
secure in his litter chair and carried over to one of the large long buildings. All such buildings
had guards in Florent uniforms standing at alert.

Willas watched curiously as Lord Alester tipped his hat, allowing the guards to fully see his
face.

“Good day, men,” Alester greeted. “I present Lord Willas Tyrell as guest this day.”

A guard at the barred door pulled on an outside chain by the doorway and it rang a bell in the
inside. In the middle of the door, a panel opened, showing a face on the other side.

“My lord, how many will enter?”

Lord Alester turned.
“If I may advise, my lord?” Alester mentioned. “There is not so much room within to easily
maneuver, given your chair.”

Ah. Willas suppressed a grimace. He decided upon the two who were carrying the chair and
one of his sworn swords to follow. The door was finally opened and Willas wondered at the
need for such security. But it made sense; his grandmother had such suspicions!

They entered into a foyer, where there was a tall, wood, unornamented Lannister clock. A
woman was seated at a desk, surrounded by paperwork, writing away. She lifted her eyes,
dipped her head in acknowledgement, and continued to work. WIllas was taken aback by this
lack of ceremony, but Lord Alester did not take notice, moving through the building with
clear familiarity. They climbed the stairs to the second floor. The lower floor of the mills had
narrow windows in the old defensive style that prevented anybody from climbing in, let alone
looking in and finding out what was inside; only the upper floors had larger glass paned
windows. The ground floors served as warehousing for the finished goods. Upper floors were
for production.

“Ah, let us show you some products with color, shall we? This room-”

Alester opened a door and Willas entered a long room, with a double row of looms facing
each other. Women worked away and Willas ruefully thought to himself that he did not know
anything at all about weaving. For all he knew, this was merely Lord Florent choosing to
allocate the labor of his lands differently; by freeing up women by having them leave their
young children under care and their older children occupied at school (why bother educating
smallfolk?) it would allow for more women to weave.

“Has a number of striped cloth and ginghams in progress. Cotton. Very popular. Good day,
weavers!”

“Good day, Lord Alester!” the women chorused back, not stopping their rhythm.

Willas could only say if asked that he saw the warp threads going up and down from pushes
of levers low on the floor controlled by the womens’ feet and thump and clack of the
mechanisms they were working with their hands. He did not know what he was looking at,
though he could understand the purpose. He approached the nearest weaver to observe. The
woman pulled on a handle connected to a dangling cord that Willas had difficulty
distinguishing from the rest of all the thread and rope and whatnot holding the entire loom
together. There was a darting movement across that caused a sharp clack. And then the
woman would pull a horizontal swinging board frame towards herself, making a thump.
From what he could tell, this was to firmly press the newest thread, the… weft? Into position.

“How many weavers do you employ?”

“Oh, fifty, at least,” Alester did not hesitate. “In this building.”

Willas could not help the surprise on his face; Lord Alester had that much available labor?
How was that possible? And what of the other buildings in this town?

“I wish to see some… fancier fabrics,” Willas tried.
Alester was very agreeable. They had to leave that particular building which seemed to only
have the more simple of patterns. The next building they entered was something different
indeed, which amazed Willas and left him entranced.

The weavers at these looms were turning out the custom brocade patterns that were so
coveted at Highgarden and by other lords. Willas approached one loom and watched as a
pattern of black prancing stags amongst black foliage on bright yellow background emerged
on a fabric using shiny, fine threads that had the sheen of satin. He looked around, trying to
figure this marvel out and could only notice that a moving belt of wooden cards with holes
punched into them in various ways must account for this difference to these looms. That, and
the sheer amount more of warp threads, lifting and dropping into position, using a series of
hooks and weights so complicated that he could not understand how it was not being
hopelessly tangled.

“We have current commissions, to ensure no waste,” Lord Alester said, surveying the room
with great satisfaction. “Granted, there is no danger of the Baratheon brocade going out of
fashion, is there?”

You don’t have to remind me of Father’s mistake, Willas snarled in his mind. I know! We all
know!

“What would it take,” Willas piped up, “to have looms such as these at Highgarden?”

Lord Alester made a cutting gesture at one of the higher ranking mill workers, a supervisor of
some sort, and she blew a whistle, a pattern of three blasts. In a trice, all work was stopped
and the weavers filed out of the room, many staring at Willas in curiosity. The doors shut
behind them. Willas shifted. He hoped his leg wouldn’t start aching, not now.

“Bellflower’s looms will not be taken,” Alester’s voice was quiet and matter of fact. “By
anyone. My lord.”

That was not what he meant at all!

“I meant that looms such as these would be worth purchasing,” Willas tried to keep his voice
level.

“They are,” Alester agreed. “Yet you must understand that outside of my desire to keep these
looms, there are other considerations.”

“And what may those be?”

“House Florent has applied for and gained royal patent from the Seven Kingdoms Patent
Office. It’s quite the idea, really. Tyrion Lannister applied for his clocks, you see. So of
course we had to investigate what the fuss was all about and well…”

Alester reached out and patted a loom with a smile.

“The Patent Office promotes the progress of science and useful arts, by securing for limited
times to authors and inventors the exclusive right to their respective writings and discoveries
for the duration of twenty years.”

He paused, looking at Willas, and Willas was embarrassed at what must be obvious confusion
on his face.

“The Crown will enforce,” Alester’s tone was cautionary. “House Florent’s right to pick and
choose how many of these looms may be built, as these are our ideas. And we wish for
exclusivity. We have twenty years to enjoy that. All others will be welcome to approach us on
the subject of purchase after that time.”

Left unsaid was that the price would be dear indeed, considering how many others would be
interested in such looms. Willas supposed he could force Lord Tarly to reveal how much it
cost him for his looms, but it was not said that these new Westerosi brocades came from
Tarly’s mills; just the usual stripes, ginghams, dots, and other less complicated patterns. He
was also nervous (though it shamed him so) at the prospect of confronting Lord Tarly.
Randyll Tarly was so fierce, so combative, so boorish that he would not take the courtesy to
ignore Willas’ lame leg. He was just the sort of man who crossed his arms in order to flex his
biceps purely to vex with intimidation while staring at Willas’ leg, daring him to do
something about it. And unfortunately, Willas got intimidated, no matter how Grandmother
scoffed at such foolish male antics.

Oh, if only Father didn’t go about saying that it was his battle strategies that won the Reach a
victory against King Robert at Ashford! To not acknowledge that it was Lord Randyll’s on
the field command that made the difference was a slight against him and his training and the
honor of his House as First in Battle and Lord Randyll would not forget, though he would not
say anything outright. Possibly the only instance of diplomacy the man had ever had the
notion to practice. Everybody knew! It put Willas on the backfoot now!

“There isn’t anything stopping anybody else from setting up weaving mills of this type,”
Willas said with some temper. “A bunch of looms and workers, that’s not patented, is it?”

“Oh, of course not,” Alester shook his head. “Having many workers in one place doing work
isn’t new. Quarries. Mines. It’s ancient, no doubt. It’s just… amusing, isn’t it, that nobody
thought to do the same for spinning and weaving.”

“Then you shan’t be surprised by new weaving mills opening, will you?” Willas challenged.

“Not at all, my lord. It was only a matter of time.”

Willas could not understand why Lord Alester was so calm about it. He thought to himself
that he should order Maester Lomys to begin work on recreating the looms that could make
brocade also. It was just luck that the Florents had a maester capable of thinking up such a
thing as that. How difficult could it be?

“And when you do open those mills, I shall have to pay a visit, to see how you’ve gone about
it, hmm?” Alester tilted his head.

Willas’ leg was aching fiercely.
“Of course,” Willas replied. “You have let me see the secret of your brocade looms after all.”

Alester nodded and smiled once more. Willas disliked it very much.

“These brocade looms are wondrous,” Willas complimented finally. “You are most
fortunate.”

“Yes, I give thanks to the Smith every day,” Alester responded.

His subsequent silence was encouraging, waiting for more inquiries. But unfortunately,
Willas had not any idea of what more he ought to ask. There was only the suspicion that
came from Lord Alester’s easy acceptance of the idea of Highgarden setting up their own
competing weaving mills. Why? The arrogance! And yet, the surety there must mean
something. As far as Willas could compare, Lord Florent must think any challenge to his
weaving mills was no challenge at all; like an experienced knight readying himself to face a
green squire in a training yard.

“Shall we continue on? There are so many other of my mills that I have not shown you, after
all,” Alester offered.

Willas gamely agreed. He was shown into a spinning mill, where a waterwheel powered rows
and rows of machines, mysterious contraptions of gears, belts, wheels, bobbins, spools, and
lengths of cotton being turned into thread. Now, he’s seen a single woman working on a
spinning wheel before and he’s seen little girl children being made to sit still and use drop
spindles; even Margaery had to do so to teach her the patience to work on embroidery later.
So the sheer speed and amount of thread being made him dumbstruck with awe. He glanced
at his guards and they were also dimly realizing the import of the machines they were
witnessing.

The cacophony of clanking and clacking was such that the workers were wearing ear
protection; headbands ending with thick cupped cork covered their ears as they walked back
and forth changing out empty spindles or full bobbins as they went. He and his guards were
given a set each to wear by Alester. They could not talk at all while in the mill. Supervisors
were told apart by the little red checkered flags they carried; waving would gain a worker’s
attention.

This one mill was dedicated to cotton. Surely another was dedicated to wool. And who
knows how many more!

Willas was starting to realize that even if others were to set up their own weaving mills, the
sheer dominance of the Florent and Tarly spinning mills were such that Lord Florent would
profit by selling the threads used in the first place!

They were turning out canvas for sails, for Royal Navy and Iron Islands Trading Company
purchase first and any extra sold on. The end cuts too small for sails were being repurposed;
made into simple shoes or sandals with cork soles. Quick, cheap, and more comfortable than
the hard wooden clogs traditionally worn by peasants. Willas did vaguely realize that nobody
in Bellflower Town went about barefoot, not even the children. And that really was
something; children usually grew so quickly that it made no sense to give them shoes at all
when it came to peasants. Or they stuffed the toes of a hand down pair from a grown up in the
family with scrap fabric and waddled around until they grew into those shoes.

There was a woolen felting mill, which was in partnership with a number of different
milliners in town. Both women and mens’ hats were being turned out in Bellflower Town,
following the styles shown in that magazine, the Lady Spectator of King’s Landing.

If men and women didn’t wish to endure the noisy clanking of a mechanical mill they were
being employed in other aspects of clothing. There were factories where ready-made clothing
were being churned out using patterns; cutters and sewers were needed for petticoats with
machine-lace trims. Aprons. Gloves. Shawls. The King’s Landing style light neck scarves.
Hoods. Cloaks. Waistcoats for both men and women. Plain white shirts or blouses which
could be customized by a woman at home with her own embroidery or the new fashion for
applique and ribbon trimming.

Mother-of-pearl buttons from the Iron Islands were brought in by the case and they were
being sewn on, some sewers specializing only on buttonholes and buttons. Others were
dedicated to hemming. Others fitted cuffs and collars. A single garment passed through
multiple hands and somehow, this was faster than a single lone worker, no matter how
experienced.

And that of course meant that there was a growing cadre of tailors and seamstresses for the
discerning merchants and their families who wanted to dress in the style of King’s Landing
with customized Florent jackets, button front long trousers, and hip-hugging long skirts and
dresses, clothes that took greater skill to create and make. These people took the time to
travel to Bellflower Town for fittings, to have their measurements taken down into large new
paper-paged ledgers in order to buy entire new wardrobes, which could be sent for
afterwards. Or the most advanced apprentices proved their worth with masterpieces and
struck out on their own, taking what they learned about pattern drafting, draping, and
customer service out into the rest of Westeros.

This was all not taking into account the waterwheel powered sawmills making lengths of
wood for the town’s roof beams, girders, and trusses, floor joists and flooring. There were the
furniture making factories, with their waterwheel powered drills, saws, belt sanders, and
lathes. The wheelhouse factory. The wheel factory. Which built the wheelhouse he was using
as Father felt the need to have all of their wheelhouses replaced with plush, upholstered,
glass-windowed, smoother-riding vehicles. Grandmother was in a fine temper over that when
she found out!

In all the ways traditional crafts worked on previously by skilled craftsmen of guilds, taking
years of scutwork and apprenticing to comprehend, learn, and become skilled at the doing
and finishing, the Florents looked for ways it could be broken apart and done more efficiently
by assembly line methods. The Florents partnered with forward-thinking masters, gave them
loans to hire on architects and builders for a factory or mill, which they were repaid with
interest and then leased those buildings to them, and set about inventing the ways to make it
happen, filing patents, which then locked these crafts masters or entire guilds into service to
the Florents (for TWENTY YEARS) by contracts and licensing fees. Were their products as
fine as true masterworks? No. Not yet. But a cheap step stool bought from Florent-owned
factories was worth coin in hand to them instead of a varnished, gilded, scrollwork cabinet
from Lannisport bought out of their control. Cheap wooden furniture was popular in Dorne,
in fact, given the lack of wood at all in many of their desert holdings!

And Willas nearly forgot the tin canning factory, turning Reach produce into Royal Navy
supplies and selling the excess off to the public!

(Lord Alester, as it turned out, dragged the tours out for so long that they hadn’t even made it
to the factories dedicated to turning out advanced farming equipment made out of steel. So
there was also that.)

There were so many, so many different ways of earning coin on Florent lands, just within
Bellflower Town. It was precious, precious, and of course Lord Florent was spending to
protect it. It did not matter in the end that Willas had seen it with his own two eyes. He was
like a child looking at a jack-in-the-box, uncomprehending of the mechanisms inside that
made the clown pop out. The Florents had kept everything secret and discreet for so, so very
long, caused his Grandmother sleepless nights, and finally showed Bellflower Town to Willas
in all its still incomplete glory. And showed that they were so far ahead in the race that there
was no point in anybody, not the Tyrells, possibly not even the Lannisters, had business
competing against them.

Willas gulped.

“Will you be staying with us for dinner, my lord?” Alester tilted his head with inquiry.

“Yes,” Willas said more firmly than he felt.

Lord Alester bowed and made a gesture at one of his guards. That man made his way to the
signal tower. Ah.

Lord Alester and his men rode alongside Willas’ wheelhouse. As they arrived, the ongoing
construction was unavoidable at Brightwater Keep. It was built upon a large hill, a traditional
motte and bailey that was improved over the generations into stone, the square towers at
corners of its wall a legacy of practical defensive architecture instead of palatial luxury that
saw Highgarden sprawl over its own hilltop in white stone. They were building out a new
encircling wall with those sharply pointed bastions, spaced a proper scorpion bolt flight range
away from the original curtain wall. Lord Florent had poured money and labor into fortifying
Bellflower Town first. Willas thought it backwards. A castle was a lord’s seat and pride, after
all!

As they crossed the new drawbridge over the new moat (still being excavated deeper) and
passed through the new gatehouse, Willas saw that the new walls incorporated new buildings
in of themselves. Long narrow blocks that served as barracks surely, armories, storerooms,
and other aggressively useful, defensive purpose.

They passed into the courtyard within the original walls, where the wheelhouse stopped and
he had to get into his litter chair. Here, it seemed that Lord Alester left the previous
improvements of his ancestors well enough alone. Willas had been made to study what the
Tyrells knew of Brightwater Keep’s layout. Past Florents had saved on labor and cost of stone
by building newer buildings along the perimeter, using the curtainwall as a fourth wall for the
buildings as time went on. The big old square stone tower keep in the center of the courtyard
had a shorter stone wing added at some point; more modern living quarters and a bigger
ballroom and feasting hall as the Florents gained slowly in wealth.

What immediately struck Willas, given the lack of obvious building activity, were that all the
upper story windows, the non-defensive ones, had glass paned windows with new storm
shutters for their protection. Waiting for him in line of precedence were Lady Melara Florent
and an entire (Too many!) troop of fosters. Now, Willas had heard that their fosterings were
unusual in that they were allowed to go home to their families for one week out of every two
moons. It didn’t seem rightly done, he thought, as the girls dipped their curtseys and the boys
made their bows as Melara named them in turn.

Willas was carried into the old great hall of Brightwater Keep, where he spied newer oil
paintings taking pride of place in place of older tapestries. He took his seat next to Lord
Alester’s right hand and Lady Melara sat at Lord Alester’s left at the high table. The fosters
were all at a separate table and doubtless because of his presence nobody else, not knights nor
the higher ranked retainers, were present for this dinner. The old grand oak table had not
changed, but the seating had; comfortable, easily moved upholstered chairs in the new Lady
Selyse style, as it was called in the Lady Spectator, showing off that Florent brocade.

The antique Myrish blown glass goblets had not changed. The porcelain plates, Westerosi-
made, were new. They were decorated with cobalt blue flowers and scrollwork patterns with
gilded rims. Very fine, indeed.

He felt safe in complimenting the appearance of these new plates, which led into a
conversation about the trip said plates had to take by sea all the way from Gulltown, doubling
the Dornish cape, and up north to Oldtown, where the most dangerous part (aside from the
risk of an entire ship sinking) were the shipping crates getting too violently jostled on the
road.

Willas got the feeling that Lord Florent was eager to finish up on improving his wharf, so that
any luxury goods he required would arrive more safely, on his own properly leveled and
tightly paved roads.

Willas looked around some more in the old hall, noticing that the vaulted beams with the fox
head corbels of the ceiling were all freshly painted and that the whole place was given a fresh
white lime wash, to better show off the oil paintings. It was then that he noticed that the very
wide and tall old fireplace had something new built inside it. It seemed like a square column
covered in blue ceramic tile, extending all the way up into the flue. There was an opening in
the middle, much smaller than he would have expected to heat a hall of the size he was sitting
in.

He inquired about it and instantly regretted it, as Lord Alester effusively launched into a
speech explaining the design and usefulness of the masonry heater. Something about the
fire’s heat being most efficiently stored within the bricks that made up the thing as hot air
traveled a labyrinth of passages to be released over time, requiring much less fuel wood at all
to be used. Willas sighed to himself; he knew some lords worried about the cost of candles,
but it was really boring and faintly ridiculous that Lord Florent, as rich as he was, with those
rings on his fingers, was banging on about the advantages of reducing the use of firewood!

“I’ve had them made for all the fireplaces, you see,” Alester continued, blatantly ignoring the
bored face that Willas was attempting to hide. “Snug and cozy, just the sort of thing for good
living! And so much less soot in the air and on the walls and well, everything! Simply
wonderful, you know. It was my nephew Erren’s idea; he’s going to file a patent!”

Willas suppressed a yawn.

“Oh?”

“Yes,” Melara nodded eagerly and Willas groaned inwardly. “Dragonstone Island has had to
be conservative with their forests. Necessity made him solve the problem. Can you imagine,
having to pay for imported firewood!”

“No, I can’t, actually,” Willas shrugged.

“It’s just the sort of thing we’re lucky to not have to manage at all, living in the Reach,”
Melara tittered.

“I suppose,” Willas tried for levity. “Ser Erren will open up a stove-making factory?”

The idea of shipping entire brick-made and tile-clad stoves around was funny.

“Oh, no,” Alester’s voice turned into that smug purr that caused Grandmother Olenna’s
hackles to rise. “He’ll obviously have trained and licensed stove-makers and open up
business and have them go out building out heaters by commission in the North, even the
Vale and the Iron Islands, of course. Like Tyrion Lannister with his flushing jakes!”

Ugh. What grasping mercantile talk is this?

“I see,” Willas took a sip of wine. “I congratulate Ser Erren on his ideas.”

“I’ll let him know, next I write,” Melara dimpled at him.

“Speaking of flushing jakes-” Alester’s teeth flashed in a grin.

Torture. Except with delicious food. Lord Florent was cruel indeed.

“We’ve had some installed! It is very well, especially with a new cistern I’ve had built on the
roof, for the flush. Would you like to see one?”

Seven Hells. Why?

Willas demurred, despite Alester assuring him that the flushing action was something to see.
The quality of the food and Melara’s less technical and therefore charming conversation was
such that it was impossible to leave before sunset. He was forced to have a raven sent to
Highgarden, stating that he would be partaking of Florent hospitality.
At the end of dinner, everybody withdrew to a large parler, where luckily Lord Alester was
enough of a good host to leave him be and the fosters approached him, as was polite and
Willas took the time to address them and inquire about their stay. They liked Brightwater
Keep. The boys liked their training, though they did not enjoy being made to run laps, push
ups, burpees (what is that?) and other physical conditioning exercises, but that was to be
expected. They gossiped as boys did about the strongest knights at Brightwater Keep and
which ones might be worth squiring for and perhaps there were better knights from their own
homes that their fathers would find for them to squire for, and attending future tourneys and
how exciting it all was.

It was a duty to address all who met with him, so he cautiously spoke to the girls. A fair few
blushed and went tongue-tied, which flattered him, but he knew not to get any ideas.
Grandmother made sure of that! They liked singing and dancing, a fair few liked riding out
for hammerball and even played soccer. He was a little baffled at that, until a very quiet girl,
Tysha Oldflowers, pointed out that no less than Queen Cersei enjoyed hammerball. With an
endorsement such as that, girls wanting to be fashionable for a potential invite to the Foxhole
as guest for royal court events had no choice but to have riding habits made and to work on
their hammer swinging skills and horsemanship.

Won’t Margaery be annoyed by that, Willas thought to himself. She didn’t much like going
faster than a trot on a palfrey.

Willas wistfully agreed that hammerball seemed quite the fun new thing to do.

He did miss riding.

They asked him if he’d been to King’s Landing. Willas had to truthfully say that he had never
left the Reach. Though, he did exchange letters with Prince Oberyn Martell. He was then
asked about any mention of King’s Landing from Prince Oberyn’s letters. It seemed harmless
and Willas was not so blind to his own faults like his father that he couldn’t admit that he
wanted to gain approbation with some light boasting. And if that meant spreading some
gossip from letters, why not?

Tysha Lannister sat in the periphery. She noted how Lord Alester and Lady Melara were
almost too obviously giving Willas Tyrell space amongst the fosters, to have a crowd of
young people decidedly not his equals, nor future equals in rank to lull him into lowering his
guard with small talk, so that she could work on making her own conclusions about him and
possibly learn something about Prince Oberyn Martell. She carefully dash-dotted notes while
hiding her notebook with the excess fabric of her embroidery hoop. Embroidery hoops were
enormously useful as a misdirection prop.

“So is your father planning on holding any tourneys in Highgarden soon?” Tysha ventured
during a pause in the conversation. “I’ve heard so much about Highgarden tourneys, they
must be so wonderful!”
